key_terms.definition: Pooling is a technique applied over the output features of a convolutional layer to reduce dimensionality. Pooling uses a local window to represent the output either by taking the maximum value (max pooling) or the average value (mean pooling).

Downsampling is a method used in neural networks, particularly for classification, where the high-dimensional input structure is intentionally reduced. This is done when the network does not require the full dimensional structure at every layer.

Strided operation is a method that combines convolution or pooling with downsampling into a single element. It achieves this by increasing the stride of the filter, causing it to move further than a single pixel at each step.

Dilated filter is a type of filter where certain values are set to zero, which is baked into the model. This configuration allows the filter to capture information from a larger spatial context or extent while using fewer parameters.

L04.subgoal: Analyze the trade-offs in deep learning architecture design and training

key_points.text: Modern deep learning architectures often use small filters stacked deeply to achieve large receptive fields (573, 574, 575).
The complexity of the required network often depends on the complexity of the input image (583, 584).
Increasing the input image scale to preserve fine-grained features is often a better trade-off than excessive downsampling (587, 588).
When data is limited, incorporating inductive bias (handcrafting filters) is beneficial, but with large datasets, end-to-end learning is often preferred (605, 606).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias refers to the constraints or prior knowledge that a model is designed with to guide its learning process. Inductive bias tends to be more beneficial when there is insufficient data, as it allows the system to optimize better by limiting the possible solutions.

Feature engineering is the historical process in computer vision and deep learning where researchers manually build handcrafted structures to help a system recognize objects. This approach involved combining these handcrafted structures into a larger system for recognition.

Receptive field is the area of the original input image that a specific neuron can observe after passing through multiple layers. Large receptive fields can be achieved even if the initial filters are spatially small by stacking layers.

Neural architecture search is a field of research that specifically attempts to optimize over the vast space of possible architectures. This process aims to find the best possible solution for a given task.

L04.subgoal: Define the receptive field and explain how its size and nature evolve through a deep network

key_points.text: The receptive field determines which parts of the initial input influence a specific part of the output.
Information outside the receptive field cannot influence the model's output.
Early layers typically produce fine-grained or detailed feature activations because convolutions are highly local.
Deeper layers produce more diffuse feature activations that are semantically meaningful.

key_terms.definition: Receptive field is a concept that defines what parts of the initial input have any influence on a specific part of the output. This field dictates that the model cannot receive information from outside of this defined area.

Convolutional layer is a type of layer in a network that performs computations using filters across input patches. These layers are fundamental components used to process input data in deep learning models.
Filter is a single component used in crafting a convolutional layer. Filters are responsible for performing the specific computations that extract features from the input data.

Feature activations are the outputs of a layer that represent complex information collected from the input image. These activations can become more semantically meaningful as they pass through multiple layers of the network.

L04.subgoal: Compare encoder-decoder architectures and introduce the U-Net solution

key_points.text: Classification networks typically use filters, non-linearity, and downsampling to produce a classification output (644, 645).
Encoder-decoder architectures compress input into a low-dimensional representation and then reconstruct it using upsampling (647, 648).
The bottleneck in encoder-decoder architectures can cause the loss of fine-grained spatial structure and details (663, 665).
The U-Net architecture is designed to maintain high-resolution structure while ensuring computational efficiency (670).

key_terms.definition: Encoder-decoder architecture is a structure that processes an input by first using convolution and downsampling to create a low-dimensional representation, and then uses convolution and upsampling to reconstruct the output.
Semantic segmentation is an image-to-image task where the output space has a spatial structure, meaning it assigns meaning to every part of the image rather than just providing a single category.
U-net is an architecture designed to bridge the gap between preserving high-resolution structure and maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for image-to-image tasks.

L04.subgoal: Explain the function and power of skip connections in deep learning architectures

key_points.text: In U-Net, skip connections allow the model to retain fine-grained spatial detail while learning semantics through an information bottleneck.
ResNet uses an identity pathway in every layer, enabling the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth for a given task.
A residual connection is fundamentally defined as the output being the function of the input plus the input dimension itself.
The ability to combine information using skip connections is a valuable computational tool also utilized in self-attention within transformers.

key_terms.definition: Skip connection is a connection across different parts of an architecture that allows information to bypass intermediate layers and pass directly toward the output. This mechanism ensures the model does not have to force fine-grained spatial detail into a low-rank embedding.
U-net is an old architecture that is still widely used for semantic segmentation. This architecture is frequently employed in applications such as land cover mapping using remote sensing data.
ResNet architecture is a deep learning model that utilizes a skipped connection in every single layer. This design allows the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth required for a specific task.

Residual connection is a specific type of connection where the output of a layer is calculated by adding the layer's function output to the input dimension itself. This connection assumes that the output and the residual connection are the same size.

L04.subgoal: Apply 3D convolutions to model spatio-temporal data and understand its limitations

key_points.text: Time can be treated as an additional dimension for convolutions, such as in a single scalar input over time.
Video data, combining spatial dimensions (RGB) and temporal frames, results in a four-dimensional input suitable for 3D convolutions.
3D convolutions are commonly used for tasks like action recognition in video.
A consequence of using 3D convolutions is that the model becomes shift invariant in time.

key_terms.definition: Convolutions in time involve performing convolutions over a temporal dimension, allowing the model to build representations using time as one of the dimensions.
3D convolutions are a type of convolution that operates over both spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension, resulting in a lower dimensional representation.
Shift invariant in time is a property where the model's output remains the same regardless of when an event occurs within the temporal sequence.

L04.subgoal: Explain how positional encodings and neural fields enhance convolutional architectures

key_points.text: Positional encoding adds location information to the input of convolutional filters to address the lack of shift invariance in MLPs.
A neural field is a field that is parameterized, fully or partially, by a neural network.
NeRF is a convolutional network that maps a five-dimensional coordinate grid (position and direction) to color and volumetric density.
Convolution is a fundamental operation for processing anything that has some structure, such as time or space.

key_terms.definition: Positional encoding is a method of adding location information to the input of convolutional filters. Positional encoding is constructed separately and added to the input signal, allowing the network to incorporate positional data into the convolution.
Neural field is a field that is parameterized fully or in part by a neural network. Neural field represents a varying physical quantity across both spatial and temporal coordinates.

Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) is a popular architecture that applies a convolutional network to a map. NeRF takes a five-dimensional coordinate grid, which includes position and camera direction, as input and outputs color and volumetric density.

Convolution is a fundamental operation used for processing anything that possesses some structure, such as images or time series. Convolution involves chopping up the input into patches and applying the same function to each patch using a slide and sum operation.

L04.subgoal: Analyze the limitations and extensions of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

key_points.text: The output of NeRF is the color of an image from a specific direction, not a complete 3D model of the scene.
NeRF is trained by taking multiple images of a scene from different positions.
Classical NeRF struggles when only a few sparse images are available or when the scene is moving.
External metadata, such as GPS location, can be incorporated into architectures by concatenation or separate convolution.

key_terms.definition: Strided convolution is a method that explicitly performs both pooling and downsampling simultaneously. This technique combines two operations into a single convolutional layer.

Pooling is a function applied to a local patch that is essentially the same as running a convolutional layer without learning weights. This function uses predefined operations, such as the maximum or average function, to constrain the layer.

L04.subgoal: Describe the computational challenges and modern architectures for video processing

key_points.text: Adding channels for all video frames (3D convolution) is computationally expensive and rarely worth it in temporal space.
State-of-the-art video models often downsample temporally because most actions can be recognized from a small number of frames.
Many advanced video models use a 'fast and slow' approach, combining low-dimensional temporal subsampling with periodic high-resolution inputs.
This two-pronged approach allows one model to model motion while the other models fine-grained semantic details.

key_terms.definition: 3D convolution is a method where channels for all different frames in a video are added, allowing the operation to slide like a window over time. This process effectively treats the video data as a volumetric input.

Fast and slow is a two-pronged model approach where one model handles motion using low-dimensional subsampling. A secondary channel simultaneously models fine-grained semantic details using high-resolution inputs.

L05.subgoal: Understand the role of Graph Neural Networks in introducing constraints in architecture design

key_points.text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are presented as a generalization of Convolutional Networks (ConvNets).
The lecture will cover appropriate problems for GNNs, their message-passing mechanism, and their approximation power.
GNNs are not universal in the same way that MLPs are, and this limitation is considered a source of power.
A key aspect of architecture design is adding constraints to limit a system from fitting certain types of functions.

key_terms.definition: Graph neural network is an architecture that generalizes convolutional networks and is designed to be applied to specific types of problems. Graph neural networks are a type of architecture that is being introduced in this lecture.
Message-passing algorithm is the primary method by which graph neural networks operate. This algorithm functions as a standard neural network that includes both a forward pass and a backward pass.
Approximation power refers to the capacity of a neural network to represent different types of functions. It also addresses the degree to which an architecture is universal.
Constraints are limitations added to a function approximator to rule out certain types of functions. This design choice allows the system to fit data only in specific, desired ways.

L05.subgoal: Classify real-world problems that can be modeled using graph structures

key_points.text: Graph Neural Networks are appropriate for problems that naturally exist on graphs or involve data types that exist on a graph.
Graph problems can be categorized by the type of question asked, such as classifying a specific node or analyzing properties of the entire graph.
Graphs are used extensively in biology and chemistry to represent molecules, where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges.
Graph Neural Networks can be used to find heuristics and approximate algorithms to solve complex graph search problems faster than classical methods.

key_terms.definition: Graph nets are an appropriate technology for solving problems that naturally exist on graphs. They are used to learn properties of nodes and edges within a graph structure to make predictions.

Node classification problem is a task where a question is asked about a specific node within a graph. This involves predicting a property or category for that individual node, such as whether a person likes a certain type of music.

Graph prediction problem involves asking a question about the entire graph structure, such as a molecule. This type of problem aims to predict properties based on the overall arrangement of atoms and bonds.
Probabilistic graphical model is a classical idea for representing probability distributions using a graph structure. Graph nets are appropriate for representing things like these distributions.
Discrete optimization is a type of problem where decision variables are being optimized. The goal is to find a setting for these variables that satisfies a system of constraints.

L05.subgoal: Compare classical algorithms to GNNs and define graph representation methods

key_points.text: Classical algorithms guarantee the true solution but may be slow, whereas GNNs can potentially learn faster approximate solutions (147, 148, 150).
A graph is represented by a set of nodes, each having an attribute vector, and an adjacency matrix representing the edges (155, 156, 165).
GNNs learn a function that maps the observed node attributes and edge structure to informative embedding vectors or predictions (176).
Node embeddings are vectors learned for each individual node, while graph embeddings are a single vector representing the entire graph (185).

key_terms.definition: Graph Neural Network (GNN) is a type of network that learns a function from the set of observed graph node attributes and the adjacency matrices to produce embedding vectors or predictions about the nodes or the entire graph.
Node embedding is a vector that is learned specifically for each individual node within a graph. This vector provides information of interest about that particular node.
Graph embedding is a single vector that is learned to represent the entire graph. This vector allows for questions to be asked about the properties of the whole graph.
Attribute vector is a vector that accompanies every node and serves as the initial input data to the graph processing algorithm. This vector contains observations about that specific node.
Adjacency matrix is a representation used to describe the edges between nodes in a graph. This matrix serves as an additional input to the graph neural network.

L05.subgoal: Explain the necessity of permutation invariance and equivariance when processing graph data

key_points.text: Representing graph data by serializing the adjacency matrix and node attributes into a single vector for an MLP is flawed because the resulting prediction depends on the arbitrary indexing of the nodes.
For graph-structured data, the processing function must be permutation-invariant to the ordering of nodes, meaning the structure does not depend on node indexing.
Permutation invariance is required when predicting a property of the entire graph, while permutation equivariance is required when predicting properties for individual nodes.
Permutation matrices (P) are used to mathematically represent reindexing of the adjacency matrix and the node attribute matrix.

key_terms.definition: Adjacency matrix is a matrix that describes the connectivity of a graph, where a value of 1 indicates an edge exists between two nodes and a value of 0 indicates no edge.

Permutation invariance is a property where a function produces the same output regardless of how the input nodes are indexed or ordered. This means the structure of the graph does not depend on the arbitrary ordering of its nodes.

Permutation equivariance is a property where if the input data is permuted (reindexed), the output predictions are permuted in the exact same way. This ensures that shuffling the nodes results in a corresponding shuffle of the predictions.
Attribute vector is the observed data associated with a single node in the graph. This vector provides specific information about that node.
Permutation matrix is a matrix used to reorder the rows and columns of another matrix. Applying this matrix changes the indexing of the nodes without changing the underlying structure of the graph.

L05.subgoal: Compare the architectural differences and commonalities between Graph Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks

key_points.text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are essentially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) applied to non-grid topologies, generalizing the concept to arbitrary graphs.
A key difference is that GNNs must handle variable neighborhood sizes, unlike CNNs which operate on fixed-shape grids.
GNNs are permutation invariant, meaning the operation does not depend on the spatial location of a node, unlike CNNs which rely on spatial dimensionality.
Both CNNs and GNNs are based on local operations, where information is aggregated from immediate neighbors to update a node's representation.

key_terms.definition: Local operation is a mechanism where data representation is updated by running local filters or computations. Every node in the graph receives input only from its immediate neighbors.
Node attribute vector is the set of feature values associated with a specific node in the graph. This is equivalent to the channels found at a point in a grid-based network.

L05.subgoal: Explain the two-step message passing mechanism used in Graph Neural Networks

key_points.text: A Graph Net layer consists of two steps: passing messages from nodes to neighbors, and aggregating those messages to update each node's representation.
The aggregate function must be permutation-invariant, meaning the output message is the same regardless of the order of the neighbor inputs.
The aggregate function is a multiset function that takes a set of items (node vectors) and produces a single output vector.
Common aggregate functions include summation, average, and max or min, which is analogous to pooling in convolutional networks.
Each application of the two-step process increases the node's receptive field by one.

key_terms.definition: Aggregate function is a function that takes a set of node vectors from a node's neighbors and produces a single message vector. This function must be permutation-invariant, meaning the output does not change regardless of the order of the input vectors.

Update function is a process that modifies a node's vector representation. It combines the information received from neighbors (messages) with the node's existing self-knowledge to refine its representation.

Permutation-invariant describes a function whose output remains the same even if the input items are reordered. This property ensures that the order in which neighbors are indexed does not affect the resulting message.

Multiset function is the technical name for a function that takes a set of items, which may contain duplicates, and maps them to a vector. This concept is used when the input node vectors might not be unique.

L05.subgoal: Define the components and theoretical constraints of message-passing graph networks

key_points.text: Classical graph problems, such as Bellman-Ford, can be represented using GNNs that rely on aggregate and update operations.
Permutation invariance is necessary when the order of inputs does not affect the optimal prediction or outcome.
A combination of an MLP and summation is a universal approximator for the family of multiset functions.
A complete graph net requires an aggregate function, an update function, and a final readout step to produce a graph embedding.

key_terms.definition: Permutation-invariant describes a property where the ordering of inputs does not change the optimal prediction or the result of the function. This constraint is applied when the domain requires that the sequence of inputs is irrelevant to the desired output.

Aggregate function is a mechanism used to combine information from a node's neighbors into a single representation. This function must be permutation-invariant, meaning the order in which the neighbor information is processed does not affect the final result.

Update function takes the messages received from neighbors and combines them with the node's current vector to produce a refined representation. This function is responsible for improving the node's embedding based on local graph information.

Graph network is a model that processes graph data by iteratively applying an aggregate function and an update function. This structure allows the network to generate updated node embeddings that capture information from the entire graph.

Readout is the final step in a graph network that converts the set of individual node embeddings into a single vector embedding for the entire graph. This process is essentially another multiset function applied over all nodes.

L05.subgoal: Relate message passing operations (aggregate and update) to standard neural network components

key_points.text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can be viewed as an unrolled Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) where the neurons are vectors (node embeddings).
The GNN process involves aggregating information from neighbors and applying a node-wise update function.
Transformers are a special kind of graph net, and attention is a particular kind of aggregation operator.
Message passing constitutes the forward pass, and the network is trained by backpropagating through the resulting computation graph.

key_terms.definition: Message passing is the process of unrolling message passing iterations where every step updates a set of node vectors by taking input data and combining information from neighboring nodes. This process is the forward pass through the network.

Aggregate is the function that takes all node vectors from a node's neighbors and combines them into a single D-dimensional vector. This combined vector serves as the message passed to the central node.

Update is the function that takes a node's current node embedding plus the message received from its neighbors to provide an updated representation of that node. This function provides the new embedding for the node.

Graph net is a framework where the message-passing algorithm is applied to a graph structure, allowing the network to process data by aggregating information over connected neighbors. This structure allows the network to be topologically similar to a regular neural network.

Transformer is a specific type of graph net, and the perspective presented here shows the intimate connection between the two architectures. Attention is described as a particular kind of aggregation operator within this context.

L05.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of message passing and the procedure for training Graph Neural Networks

key_points.text: Transformers are a type of graph net that uses attention as its aggregation operator.
The connectivity structure of a graph is determined by the data and is not optimized during the GNN training process.
Within a single layer of a GNN, all aggregation functions share the same weights (weight sharing).
Training data can be structured either for node-level prediction (node embeddings + edges + node label) or for graph-level prediction (whole graph + graph label).

key_terms.definition: Graph nets are a type of network that uses attention as its aggregation operator. This structure allows the network to process information across a graph using attention-based aggregation.

Aggregation operation is a method of combining messages from neighbors that is not limited to simple summing or averaging. Instead, it is called attention, which is a summation dependent on the value of the node embeddings.
Transformer is the name given to a system where the aggregation operator is attention. This system utilizes attention to aggregate information across the graph structure.

Weight sharing idea means that all the aggregate functions used in parallel across all operations within one layer of the message-passing algorithm are the same function. This allows the model to generalize across graphs of different sizes.

L05.subgoal: Explain the theoretical limitations of GNNs based on graph equivalence classes

key_points.text: GNNs cannot distinguish between all possible graphs, leading to equivalence classes where different graphs yield the same prediction (739, 740).
According to a GNN, two graphs are equivalent if they possess the same neighborhood tree structures for all nodes (758).
The discriminative power of GNNs is equivalent to the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) algorithm (790, 796).
Breaking node symmetry (e.g., by assigning a one-hot encoding based on position) allows for distinction but sacrifices permutation invariance (782, 783).

key_terms.definition: Graph net is a type of neural network designed to approximate functions defined over graph structures. Graph nets determine equivalence between graphs based on the tree structures observed during message propagation.
Equivalence class is a set of graphs that a graph net cannot distinguish from one another. If two graphs belong to the same equivalence class, the graph net must assign the same prediction to both.

Tree structure is the local neighborhood pattern that a node observes when updating its representation based on incoming messages. This structure forms the entire characterization of the graph from the perspective of a graph net.

Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm is a classical graph theory algorithm that takes two graphs and decides whether they are structurally the same or different. The power of a graph net to distinguish graphs is limited by the capabilities of this algorithm.

Permutation invariance is the property where a model remains unchanged regardless of the ordering of the nodes in the graph. Graph nets are designed to be invariant to the ordering of the nodes, but breaking this symmetry can be a trade-off.

L05.subgoal: Explain the theoretical limits and practical requirements of Graph Neural Networks

key_points.text: Using a universal approximator (like MLP) is necessary to approximate all desired multiset functions.
Choosing an aggregation function (e.g., mean instead of sum) can cause the model to fail if the true function requires information lost by that choice.
Conventional GNNs have fundamental limits, such as being unable to estimate the graph diameter.
These fundamental limits can be overcome by adding positional encodings to break the symmetry of the graph net.

key_terms.definition: Universal approximator is a function or network that has the theoretical capacity to approximate any function within a specified set of functions. For example, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is stated to be a universal approximator to any multiset function.

Graph net is a type of neural network specifically designed for processing data that is structured as a graph. Graph nets are appropriate for handling graph-structured data, though they have fundamental limits on the properties they can estimate.

Positional encoding is a method used to break the symmetry of a graph net by providing each node with a vector that indicates its location within the graph. This allows the network to discriminate between graphs that otherwise have the same neighborhood structure.

Aggregation function is the operation used within a graph net to combine information received from a node's neighbors. The choice of this function, such as sum or mean, can fundamentally affect the network's ability to learn the true function.

Generalization refers to a model's ability to perform well on new, unseen data, which is distinct from merely fitting the training data. A model that only fits the training data may not generalize well to real-world scenarios.

L06.subgoal: Outline the fundamental questions and scope of deep learning generalization theory

key_points.text: Deep neural networks generalize to some degree, but the underlying reasons for this generalization are not fully understood.
Classical theories of generalization do not adequately explain the observed performance of deep learning models.
The generalization properties of deep networks are considered one of the biggest open questions in AI research.
The lecture will cover the definition of generalization, the generalization capabilities of deep nets, and the failures of classical theories.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on data that it has not encountered during the training process. This concept addresses whether a model's learned patterns apply successfully to new, unseen examples.
Approximation refers to the process of modeling or representing functions. This is the foundational topic that precedes the discussion of whether those models can successfully generalize.

Inductive biases are the inherent preferences of a network toward certain types of solutions. These preferences guide the network to favor solutions that generalize well over those that merely fit the training data.

L06.subgoal: Distinguish between empirical risk, population risk, and the concept of generalization

key_points.text: Approximation focuses on minimizing the empirical risk, which measures the fit to the training data.
Population risk (test error) measures how well a model performs on new samples from the data generating process p.
Machine learning can be factored into three topics: approximation, optimization, and generalization.
Generalization is defined as the gap between the training error and the test error.

key_terms.definition: Empirical risk is the average loss incurred over all of the available training data points. This measure quantifies how well a model fits the specific data it was trained on.
Population risk is the expected error when making predictions on new samples drawn from the entire data generating process. This represents how well the model performs in the real world.
Empirical test risk is the error measured specifically over a finite sample, such as a designated test set. This provides a practical estimate of the model's performance on unseen data.
Generalization is the difference between the error observed on the training data and the error observed on the test data. This gap determines how well a model performs on new, unseen observations.

L06.subgoal: Analyze how data and model structure influence generalization error

key_points.text: Training data must represent the full variation of the real-world distribution for a model to generalize well.
A memorization model, such as a filing cabinet, achieves zero approximation error but typically has high generalization error.
Some functions can fit training data well by chance without having a true underlying model, leading to poor out-of-sample predictions.
The central question of the course is whether deep neural networks possess generalization capabilities.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on new, unseen data that comes from the same underlying distribution as the training data. If the training set does not represent all the variations encountered in the world, the model will not generalize well.
Generalization error is the difference between the empirical risk and the population risk. It measures how well a model performs on data outside of the training set.

Approximation error is the error rate of a model when it is able to retrieve the exact memorized answer for every data point it was trained on. This error is zero if the model perfectly memorizes the training data.

Memorization is the process where a model simply stores and retrieves the exact answers from its training data. This behavior is characteristic of models like the filing cabinet, which do not learn underlying patterns.

Data distribution is the underlying statistical pattern of the data that the model is trained on. Understanding this distribution is critical because if the training set does not represent all the interesting aspects of variation, generalization will fail.

L06.subgoal: Design and apply experiments to distinguish deep net generalization from pure memorization

key_points.text: Generalization refers to how a model performs on unseen data, while memorization refers to what the model predicts on the training data points.
A counting experiment can estimate the required size of a 'filing cabinet' (a pure memorization model) needed to achieve a certain prediction accuracy.
Applying this experiment to LLMs suggests that the required cabinet size (100 trillion) exceeds the known training data size, implying non-memorization.
Applying the experiment to text-to-image models suggests a required cabinet size of 12 trillion, also indicating non-memorization.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to make predictions on data points that were not included in the original training set. This process involves determining what the model does when presented with unseen data.

Memorization is the process where a model simply predicts the exact output for every data point it encountered during training. This behavior is defined by what the model predicts specifically on the training data points.
Filing cabinet is a simple model type that memorizes training data by predicting specific values only for the points it has seen. For all other points, the filing cabinet predicts zero.

Deep net is a complex neural network that achieves approximation error by interpolating and extrapolating from the training data. This method of function fitting is markedly different from the simple memorization of a filing cabinet.

Large Language Model (LLM) is a family of advanced deep nets, such as ChatGPT, that are capable of complex prediction tasks. These models are used to process sequences of words as input and generate predictions.

L06.subgoal: Illustrate out-of-distribution generalization using deep learning examples

key_points.text: Deep neural networks can be trained to map inputs, such as sketches, to corresponding outputs, such as photos of cats.,
Classical machine learning generalization assumes that data points are independently and identically sampled (IID) from the same population.,
The deep net project demonstrated generalization even when presented with hand-drawn cats, which were out-of-distribution (OOD) relative to the training data.,
This ability to generalize to OOD data suggests a form of 'creativity' or a mechanism in deep learning that is not fully understood.,

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform successfully on data it has never been trained on. This concept is demonstrated when a model works even when given inputs that are systematically different from its training set.
Out-of-distribution input refers to data that is systematically different from the data the model was trained on. These inputs are outside the scope of the training population.
Edge detector is a tool, specifically HED, used in the project as a proxy for what a human might have drawn. It is used instead of expensive human-hand-drawn sketches.

L06.subgoal: Explain how architectural biases enable generalization in deep learning models

key_points.text: ConvNets process input by chopping it into patches and independently processing each patch (S309, S310).
Decomposing a problem into independent components results in compositionality (S311).
Architectural constraints and biases allow models to achieve certain feats of generalization (S316).
Graph nets can generalize to new permutations of inputs because they are permutation-invariant or equivariant (S317, S318).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias refers to the architectural constraints and biases built into a model that allow it to perform certain feats of generalization. These biases enable the model to generalize beyond what is strictly predicted by naive statistical learning theory.

Compositionality is a property where a system can take a new composition of things and factor them into independent components, such as patches. This allows the system to know what to do because it only needs to imitate the training data on those individual components.

Permutation-invariant describes an architectural property where a model can generalize to new permutations of its inputs. This means the model does not need to have seen every possible permutation during training to perform correctly.

L06.subgoal: Explain the role of Occam's razor in generalization theory and its mathematical limitations

key_points.text: Occam's razor suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.
The principle requires that the model must fit the data; otherwise, the statement is absurd.
A rigorous version of Occam's razor states that the shortest program that generates the data will generalize best.
Finding the shortest program is computationally intractable because it requires searching over the space of all possible programs.

key_terms.definition: Occam's razor is a principle stating that among competing explanations that fit the data equally well, one should prefer the simplest model. This principle suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.
Generalization theory is the study of how well a model trained on a specific dataset will perform when applied to unseen data. This theory is based on variations of Occam's razor.

A heuristic is a practical approach or rule of thumb that is not rigorously proven but is used to guide decision-making. The initial statement regarding Occam's razor is considered a heuristic because measuring 'simplest' and 'generalization' requires mathematical precision.

The shortest program is a concept from algorithmic information theory that serves as a rigorous version of Occam's razor. This program is the one that perfectly fits or generates the data and is predicted to generalize best.

An equivalence class is a set of models that are considered equal because they all fit the data equally well. This concept is used to define the scope of models when discussing the quote 'all models are wrong, but some are useful.'

L06.subgoal: Compare classical overfitting with the phenomenon of double descent in high-capacity models

key_points.text: Classical overfitting occurs when increasing model capacity allows the model to fit noise in the data rather than the true underlying function.
Double descent is the phenomenon where, after initial overfitting, increasing model capacity further can lead to better generalization error.
High-capacity models are hypothesized to contain two components: a simple, generalizing fit and a spiking component that memorizes noise.

key_terms.definition: Overfitting is the scenario where a model fits to properties of the training data that do not generalize, such as noise. This causes the model to deviate wildly from the true underlying function.
Bias is the training error, which represents the error incurred when the model is trained on the data. It is one component used in the bias-variance trade-off.
Variance is the difference between the test error and the training error. It measures how much the model's predictions change when trained on different subsets of the data.

Double descent is a phenomenon where the generalization error of a model starts to improve again after initially worsening as the number of parameters increases. This suggests that the classical picture of overfitting is inaccurate.
Model capacity is the complexity of a hypothesis space, which can be measured by the number of parameters. Controlling this capacity is necessary to prevent a model from overfitting.

L06.subgoal: Explain the double descent phenomenon and its relationship to model capacity and regularization

key_points.text: Unlike polynomial regression, which has a provable closed-form solution, neural network solutions depend on random factors like initialization and mini-batches.
The double descent phenomenon describes how test error initially increases (overfitting) but then decreases again as model capacity increases past the interpolation threshold.
When a model has high capacity, implicit regularizers select the smoothest solution from the set of functions that perfectly fit the training data.
The complexity of a solution may be more accurately measured by the norm of the parameter vector rather than simply counting the number of parameters.

key_terms.definition: Double descent phenomenon describes a pattern where, after initial overfitting, increasing the model capacity eventually leads to improved generalization performance. This phenomenon involves the test error spiking after the interpolation threshold and then decreasing again.

Interpolation threshold is the point in model training where the model is capable of perfectly memorizing all the training data. This threshold marks the transition point where the model begins to fit the training data perfectly.

Inductive bias is a pressure that selects a specific solution from the set of all possible solutions that equally fit the training data. This bias often favors solutions that possess desirable properties, such as smoothness.

Overfitting is the condition where a model's training error continues to decrease, but its test error eventually begins to increase. This occurs when the model has too much capacity relative to the data.

Capacity is a measure of the complexity of a hypothesis space, which can be quantified by the number of parameters or the computational effort (flops). Higher capacity allows the model to represent more complex functions.

L06.subgoal: Compare classical generalization theories (VC theory) with the challenges posed by deep learning

key_points.text: The number of parameters is not a reliable measure of complexity because a small network can approximate a complex function using only a tiny fraction of its parameters.
VC theory posits that generalization is likely if the number of training data points is much larger than the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space.
The VC dimension (d) is defined as the maximum number of unique dichotomies (binary classifications) a model can apply to the training data.
Neural networks can achieve any possible dichotomy over a dataset, which results in an exponentially loose generalization bound that fails to explain deep learning's success.

key_terms.definition: VC dimension is a measure of capacity that counts the number of unique dichotomies a function class can apply to the training data. A higher VC dimension means the model can classify the training data in more different ways.

Dichotomy is a binary labeling of all the training data points, assigning each point to either a positive or negative class. This labeling is represented as a vector of assignments to positive one or negative one.
Hypothesis space is the set of all candidate functions or neural architectures that the learning algorithm is searching over. The size of this space is a measure of the model's capacity.

Generalization error is the difference between the error measured on the training data and the error measured on the population data. This difference indicates how well a model performs on unseen data.

VC theory is a framework that relates the size of the training data to the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space. This theory provides a guarantee that population error matches training error if the data size is sufficiently large relative to the hypothesis space size.

L06.subgoal: Explain how simplicity bias in the parameter function map drives generalization

key_points.text: Generalization requires the presence of some kind of inductive bias (690).
The version space is defined as the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the training data (711).
The parameter function map is a many-to-one mapping, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function (725).
Empirically, most random parameter settings in a neural network tend to map to simple functions (731, 744).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias is the necessary assumption or rule that allows a model to generalize beyond the training data. It is the mechanism that rules out solutions that merely memorize the training points without making predictions about unseen samples.

The version space is the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the given training data. In neural networks, this is the set of all parameter settings that achieve zero training error.

The parameter function map is the relationship that connects the parameters (weights and biases) of a model to the actual mathematical function that the model defines. This map is many-to-one, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function.

Simplicity bias is the tendency for deep nets to favor simple or smooth solutions when multiple solutions perfectly fit the training data. This bias suggests that the model naturally gravitates toward less complex functions.

Lempel-Ziv complexity is a specific measure of function complexity used to quantify how compressible a function's output is. It relates to how well a function's output can be compressed using a compression algorithm.

L06.subgoal: Explain why deep neural networks are biased toward finding simple, low-rank solutions

key_points.text: The classical view that deeper nets have greater capacity to organize data is challenged because even deep linear nets can achieve this organization.
The core argument is that products of matrices tend to be low rank, which creates a bias toward low-rank solutions in deep networks.
Random matrix theory suggests that products of random Gaussian matrices will result in a low rank matrix.
Optimization dynamics, such as Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), can affect generalization by preferring flat minima over sharp minima.

key_terms.definition: Kernel matrix is a matrix that characterizes the representation of input data at the output of a neural network. Every row and column in this matrix represents a data point, and the value indicates the similarity between those two data points in the network's representational vectors.

Rank is a measure of a matrix indicating the number of linearly independent rows and columns it contains. Blockier matrices, which indicate clustered data, tend to have a lower rank, suggesting a simpler data format.
Effective rank is a variation of the matrix rank used to characterize the representation of data. Lower effective rank signifies a more clustered-like structure in the data representation.
Weight decay is a type of explicit regularizer used in optimization. It works by tending to shrink the weights during each update step, which helps the network learn simpler solutions.

Flat minima are basins in the objective function's energy landscape where the loss is low over a large region of the parameter space. These flat minima are argued to generalize better than narrow minima.

L06.subgoal: Explain how architectural symmetries, factorization, and constraints enable deep learning generalization

key_points.text: Architectural symmetries, such as translation equivariance, cause models to exhibit out-of-sample generalization.
Architectures factor the input signal into components, and the conjunction of these components is defined by the architecture, not learned.
Generalization can be achieved by fitting to data under structural constraints or domain knowledge baked into the architecture.
A core theory suggests that the shortest program that fits the data will be the one that generalizes.

key_terms.definition: Invariance is a property where a model's output remains unchanged despite a transformation of the input, such as when a max pooling operation is applied over channels. This allows the model to be insensitive to specific input orientations.

Equivariance is a property where a transformation applied to the input causes a corresponding, predictable transformation in the model's predictions. For instance, if the input nodes are permuted, the predictions will also be permuted.

Compositionality is the ability of an architecture to factor an input signal into small components, where the final output is determined by stitching together the results of these components according to the architecture's design. This conjunction of components is defined by the architecture and is,

Domain knowledge is specialized information, such as equations of perspective projection or light transport, that is intentionally built into a neural architecture. This allows the model to generalize by using inherent structures rather than merely fitting the training data.

Shortest program is the theoretical concept that posits the program which fits the data most concisely will be the one that generalizes best. This idea suggests that a program that is short enough to fit the data will possess generalization capabilities.

L07.subgoal: Identify optimization as the primary unsolved challenge in deep learning

key_points.text: Deep learning problems are traditionally framed by questions regarding approximation, finding a solution, and generalization.
Approximation and generalization are currently considered largely solved by using large transformers and massive datasets.
Optimization is the primary area of improvement in deep learning.
The lecture will cover classical optimization approaches and discuss making training scalable.

key_terms.definition: Optimization is the process of making the training of a deep learning model as efficient as possible. It is the primary focus area for improvement when the other puzzle pieces are addressed.

L07.subgoal: Define the components of a deep learning loss function and explain the optimization process

key_points.text: A loss function measures the discrepancy between the neural network's prediction and the target value, averaged over the training data set.
The primary goal of training is to find the weights (W) that minimize the defined loss function.
Optimization is achieved by iteratively moving weights downhill using the gradient descent operation.
Challenges in training large models include high-dimensional optimization due to many weights and the complexity of very deep networks.
For the scope of this lecture, the stochastic gradient problem is ignored, assuming the ability to evaluate the true gradient on all data at every step.

key_terms.definition: Neural network is a function that takes inputs and weights and produces an output. This function is the core component of the model being trained.

Loss function is a classic machine learning function that measures the discrepancy between the neural network's output and the target value across the dataset. This function is typically averaged over all the training data points.

Gradient descent is an iterative operation where weights are moved downhill on the loss function to find the place with the smallest loss. This process involves computing gradients and adjusting weights to minimize the error.
Learning rate is the step size, denoted as eta, which determines how large the steps are when moving the weights during the gradient descent operation.
Stochastic gradients are noisy estimates of the full gradient across all data points. These estimates are computed by calculating gradients only on a small handful of data points in each iteration.

L07.subgoal: Identify the challenges of scaling neural network width and depth

key_points.text: Scaling a neural network's width improves performance (achieves better loss), but it causes the optimal learning rate to change.
Naively scaling a neural network's depth often results in worse performance, which is undesirable.
Residual architectures are a primary technique used to fix the performance issues associated with deep networks.
Modern literature and fixes can eliminate the optimization drift that occurs when scaling networks.

key_terms.definition: Scaling refers to increasing the size of a neural network, which can be achieved by making the network wider or by making the network deeper. This process is done to improve the overall performance of the network.
Training loss is a metric that is plotted to show the performance of the network during the training process. It is used to observe how the network performs as its size or learning rate changes.
Learning rate is a hyperparameter that determines the step size used during the training process. The optimal learning rate changes when the model is scaled up.
Residual architecture is a design technique used to fix scaling problems in deep networks. Using this architecture helps maintain performance even when the network is made deeper.
Scaling the width involves making the neural network wider, which is one method of increasing network size. This scaling generally leads to a better achieved loss, improving performance.

L07.subgoal: Compare first and second order optimization methods and their underlying assumptions

key_points.text: First order methods rely solely on first derivatives (gradients) of the loss function.
Second order methods utilize both first and second derivatives of the loss function.
The gradient (g) is a vector, and the Hessian (h) is a matrix of second derivatives.
The lecture will explain the modeling assumptions and potential shortcomings of different optimization approaches.

key_terms.definition: First order methods are optimization algorithms that rely exclusively on using the first derivatives of the loss function. These methods are the type of approach commonly used in deep learning.

Second order methods are optimization algorithms that utilize both the first and the second derivatives of the loss function. These methods are distinguished by their use of second derivatives in addition to the first derivatives.
The gradient is the derivative of the loss with respect to the weights, which is the quantity obtained by performing back propagation. It is conceptually treated as one large vector.
The Hessian is a matrix of second derivatives that corresponds to all possible pairs of second derivatives. It is a matrix representation of the second derivatives of the loss function.
The second derivative is a big matrix of second derivatives of the loss function with respect to the weights. This matrix is used by second order methods.

L07.subgoal: Derive and critique Newton's method for optimization in deep learning

key_points.text: The loss function is approximated using a Taylor expansion, which separates the linearization (first order) and the nonlinear part (higher order).
Newton's method is an optimization algorithm that uses both first-order (gradient) and second-order (Hessian) information.
A major problem with Newton's method is that the Hessian matrix is d by d, making it too large to store or invert in large neural networks.
Newton's method only finds a critical point of the quadratic form, which could potentially be a maximum rather than a minimum.

key_terms.definition: Taylor expansion is a method where different classical approaches to optimization take the loss function and approximate it using a series expansion. This expansion allows the loss function to be analyzed by breaking it down into different order terms.
Hessian matrix is a d by d matrix that represents the second-order term in the Taylor expansion of the loss function. This matrix describes the curvature of the loss function in the weight space.

Newton's method is an optimization algorithm that uses both first and second-order information to determine an optimization step. It is described as preconditioning the gradient with the inverse Hessian.
Linearization of our loss function refers to the first-order term of the Taylor expansion. This term is defined as the gradient inner product delta w.

Quadratic form is the mathematical structure that the Taylor expansion takes when it is calculated up to the second order. This form is used when minimizing the loss function with respect to the weight perturbation delta w.

L07.subgoal: Derive the Gauss-Newton decomposition and understand the resulting optimization method

key_points.text: The full Hessian of a composite objective function decomposes into two pieces, known as the Gauss-Newton decomposition. (Subject)
The Gauss-Newton method simplifies the Hessian by assuming the second derivative related to the model's curvature is negligible. (Subject)
The Gauss-Newton method uses an iterative weight update rule: delta w is minus h inverse g. (Subject)

key_terms.definition: Gauss-Newton decomposition is a formula derived for the second derivative of a composite objective function. This decomposition splits the full Hessian into two pieces based on the product rule.

A composite objective function is a function that is the composition of two other functions. This structure is common in machine learning, such as when combining an error function and a neural network.
The Gauss-Newton method is an algorithm derived from the Gauss-Newton decomposition. It provides an iterative weight update using a specific form of the Hessian.

Squared error is a specific error measure that is often assumed in the context of the Gauss-Newton method. For this measure, the second derivative with respect to the model is simplified to a constant value.

L07.subgoal: Explain the practical challenges of advanced optimization methods and gradient calculation

key_points.text: Advanced optimization methods are often avoided because they require computationally expensive steps like inverting matrices and computing extra derivatives.
When inverting a matrix, a common practice to improve conditioning is adding a small identity matrix to the matrix.
Standard backpropagation implicitly calculates the gradient without explicitly forming the partial derivative of the loss function with respect to the weights.
While forward mode automatic differentiation can compute both the gradient and the partial derivative, it is significantly more expensive than standard backpropagation.

key_terms.definition: Gauss-Newton method is an optimization technique that requires both inverting matrices and computing extra derivatives. This method is often used in contexts where a low rank Gaussian approximation is present.

Low rank Gaussian approximation is a mathematical assumption where the approximation used in the model has a low rank. This condition can be a reason why certain optimization methods might be desirable.
Forward mode automatic differentiation is a technique used for calculating derivatives, which is noted to be significantly more computationally expensive than backpropagation.

Extra derivatives are additional derivatives that must be computed when using certain optimization methods, beyond the standard regular gradient. These computations, along with matrix inversion, are practical drawbacks of certain methods.
Regular gradient is the standard gradient computed during optimization, which is typically calculated implicitly through the process of backpropagation.

L07.subgoal: Compare how different norms influence the resulting steepest descent optimization algorithm

key_points.text: Matrix operations like inversion or Singular Value Decomposition are significantly more computationally expensive than performing forward or backward passes in a neural network.
Backpropagation avoids explicitly forming large derivative tensors by only tracking derivatives with respect to the loss, which is a single number.
Steepest descent is a technique that models the unknown nonlinear part of the loss function by replacing it with a known quadratic term, $\lambda/2$.
When the L2 (Euclidean) norm is used in steepest descent, the resulting algorithm is equivalent to standard gradient descent with a specific step size.
Using the infinity norm in steepest descent results in a distinct algorithm known as sine gradient descent.

key_terms.definition: Steepest descent is an optimization technique where the nonlinear part of a function is replaced with a known, simpler function to facilitate the optimization process. This method involves choosing a specific norm to measure the distance of the weight change.
The Euclidean norm is a specific measure of distance used in optimization, where a ball of fixed Euclidean norm is represented by a circle or a sphere. This norm is equivalent to the L2 norm.
The infinity norm is a measure that determines the maximum size of a vector across all its coordinates. When using this norm, the unit ball takes on the shape of a square.

Gradient descent is a vanilla form of optimization algorithm that results from applying L2 geometry to the optimization space. It is a specific outcome of the steepest descent method when using the Euclidean norm.

Taylor expansion is a mathematical tool used in optimization to approximate a function by throwing away the nonlinear part. This expansion is used to set up the optimization problem for steepest descent.

L07.subgoal: Analyze how norms and bounds can guarantee the stability of optimization algorithms

key_points.text: The solution to the steepest descent problem can be separated into computing the step size and computing the direction.
Every norm has a corresponding dual norm, which is relevant in optimization formulations.
Approximations, such as replacing the loss function with a norm, do not guarantee the validity of the solution.
Guarantees can be achieved by upper-bounding the Taylor expansion using a linear piece and finding a suitable lambda and norm.
The instructor's current research focuses on applying these bounding techniques to complex models like multi-layer neural networks.

key_terms.definition: Dual norm is a concept that every norm has, and it appears in the general formulation of the solution to the steepest descent problem.
Steepest descent problem is an optimization problem whose solution can be separated into two distinct parts: computing the step size and computing the direction.
Taylor expansion is a mathematical tool that holds true when the loss function is analytic, allowing for the approximation of the function.
Loss function is the function used in optimization, and it can be replaced by a favorite norm when deriving different optimization algorithms.

L07.subgoal: Explain why non-Euclidean norms are necessary for optimization in non-isotropic weight spaces

key_points.text: The assumption that the gradient direction is always optimal assumes the weight space is isotropic, where all axes are equal.
In deep learning, the loss function space may be non-isotropic, meaning different directions in the weight space are not equal.
Using a different norm is equivalent to scaling each coordinate differently, similar to using a preconditioner matrix,.
The idea of building a norm is to capture at what rate the linear approximation of the loss function breaks down when moving in different directions,.

key_terms.definition: Norm is a mathematical function used to measure the magnitude of a vector or the difference between vectors. Norms allow for different weightings of coordinate directions, which is crucial when analyzing optimization steps.

Steepest descent is an optimization algorithm that decomposes the movement into a step size and a step direction. The direction chosen determines how the algorithm moves toward minimizing the loss function.

Non-isotropic space is a mathematical space where the axes are not equal to each other, meaning that different directions have different scales or magnitudes. This condition arises when the loss function does not have the property that all directions in the weight space are equal.
Preconditioner matrix is a tool used to scale each coordinate in the weight space at a different rate. This scaling allows the optimization process to account for the non-uniform nature of the space.

L07.subgoal: Define and apply matrix norms to control the size of weight updates

key_points.text: The goal of gradient descent is to find an optimal step size (Goldilocks step size) for weight updates.
Since neural networks are built from matrices, the size of weight updates should be measured using a matrix norm.
A matrix norm provides the necessary scale to quantify whether a weight update is too large or too small.
Examples of matrix norms include the Frobenius norm and the Spectral norm, which is the largest singular value.

key_terms.definition: Matrix norm is a mathematical tool used to measure the size or scale of a matrix. It allows researchers to quantify whether a weight update is too big or too small.
Frobenius norm is one specific example of a matrix norm used to measure the size of a neural network's weight matrices.
Spectral norm is a type of matrix norm defined as the largest singular value of a matrix.
Nuclear norm is one of the specific types of matrix norms available for measuring the size of a matrix.
Schatten p-norms represent a general class of norms that can be used to measure the size of a matrix.

L07.subgoal: Define and compare various matrix norms used to measure neural network stability

key_points.text: Neural networks can be analyzed using a spectral perspective by decomposing weight matrices into their Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).
The spectral norm of a matrix M is defined as the maximum L2 norm of the output vector MV, given that the input vector V has a unit L2 norm.
The spectral norm can be generalized to an induced operator norm by allowing arbitrary norms on the input and output spaces.
The RMS-to-RMS operator norm is a natural choice for neural network layers because normalizing activations using the RMS norm keeps coordinates well-behaved.
The RMS-to-RMS induced operator norm is equivalent to the spectral norm, differing only by a dimensional factor.

key_terms.definition: Singular Value Decomposition is a generalized eigenvalue decomposition that every matrix possesses. This decomposition allows one to mentally break down each weight matrix in a neural network.

Spectral norm is a way of measuring the size of a matrix, which is equivalent to the largest singular value of the weight matrix. Formally, it is the maximum L2 norm of the output vector when the input vector has a unit L2 norm.

Induced operator norm is a way to define a norm on a matrix based on specific norms chosen for the input and output spaces. This definition is achieved by specifying a norm on the input space and a norm on the output space.
RMS norm is a rescaled Euclidean norm for a vector. Specifically, it is defined as the L2 norm of the vector scaled by the inverse of the square root of the dimension.

RMS to RMS operator norm is the induced operator norm applied to a matrix when both the input and output vector spaces are equipped with the RMS norm. This norm measures the maximum RMS norm of the output given a unit RMS norm input.

L07.subgoal: Explain how using specific norms solves the width scaling problem in neural networks

key_points.text: Defining a particular norm is the method that solves the width scaling problem in neural networks.
To remove drift in the optimal learning rate, weights must be initialized and updates must be performed such that their RMS-to-RMS operator norm is around 1.
Normalizing the initial matrix controls the RMS norms as features move through the network, ensuring bounded output features.
Controlling the norm of updates ensures that the change in activation vectors from one step to the next is controlled.
The constraints are applied only at initialization and between consecutive steps, which prevents damage to the network's expressivity over many steps.

key_terms.definition: Operator norm is a mathematical measure that provides an upper-bound on how much the features of a particular layer can change. This norm does not guarantee that the features will change by this amount, only that they cannot change more than this amount.
Width scaling problem is the issue that defining a particular norm helps to solve, specifically related to maintaining stable training when varying the width of a neural network.

RMS to RMS operator norm is a specific norm used to initialize and update weight matrices such that the norm of the matrix or update is around 1. This normalization helps control RMS norms as data moves through the network.
Expressivity is the capacity of the neural network to approximate functions, and the goal is to constrain network properties without damaging this approximation capacity.

L07.subgoal: Explain scaling rules for network width and depth to ensure stable training

key_points.text: Using a non-dimensional norm (like RMS norm) keeps the size of individual coordinates invariant to the layer width, which helps stabilize the system.
Normalizing updates in a specific norm allows the optimal learning rate to be independent of the network width.
For deep networks, scaling factors are necessary to prevent the dynamics from either blowing up or going to zero as the depth increases.
In transformer architectures, the standard practice is to divide by the square root of the number of blocks (L) because the blocks are considered incoherent, similar to a random walk.

key_terms.definition: RMS norm is a non-dimensional norm used to control the size of activations within a layer. This norm keeps the size of the individual coordinates invariant to the layer's width.

Well-scaled depth limit is a condition where a compound system, composed of many terms, remains stable when the number of terms approaches infinity. This stability is achieved by carefully scaling the internals of the system.

Residual network is an architecture where a single block takes an input $x$ and returns $x$ plus the block's output of $x$. This structure allows for the composition of many blocks while maintaining a nice function.
Block multiplier is a factor placed in front of blocks within a residual network. This factor is crucial for ensuring that the network's dynamics do not blow up or go to zero as the depth increases.

L07.subgoal: Describe the modular framework for building optimization theory into neural network architectures

key_points.text: The goal is to build a modular optimization theory that can cover the vast variety of neural network architectures (747, 749).
A module is an abstraction representing a component (layer or full network) defined by its input space, output space, and weight space (754, 757).
Each module must be equipped with a norm, which is a function mapping its weight space to the real numbers (771).
When composing two modules, the forward function is achieved through function composition, and the backward function uses the chain rule (780, 782).
The central theoretical problem is finding a way to automatically combine the norms of constituent modules into a norm for the composite module (785, 793).

key_terms.definition: A module is an abstraction that handles inputs in an input space, outputs in an output space, and possesses weights in a weight space. Modules can represent either an individual layer or a full neural network.
An atomic module is one of the basic layer types that forms the library, such as ReLU, linear, convolution, or embedding. These modules are the fundamental building blocks of the network.
A norm is a function that maps a module's weight space to the real numbers. This function is used to equip the module with a measure of its properties.
A forward function is the function that the module expresses, which represents the primary operation of the module. This function dictates how the module processes its inputs.
A backward function is the derivatives of the forward function. This function is necessary for computing the derivatives during optimization.

L08.subgoal: Identify the core concepts and current relevance of the Transformer architecture

key_points.text: Transformers are the current architecture that is highly relevant for job prospects.
The Transformer architecture is based on three key ideas: operating over tokens, attention, and positional encoding.
Attention is the only truly new concept in the Transformer architecture.
The lecture will use the theme that context can give the same information entirely new meaning.

key_terms.definition: Transformer is a specific concrete instantiation of an architecture that the lecture will focus on, contrasting with the general class of functions found in graph nets.
Attention is the key concept that is genuinely new to the field, while other components of the transformer are merely new names for existing ideas.
Positional encoding is one of the three key ideas behind transformers that the lecture will discuss further, and it is a concept the students have encountered previously.
Token is the unit of data over which the transformer operates, representing the fundamental input element.

L08.subgoal: Explain why CNNs struggle with global relationships due to their inherent locality bias

key_points.text: CNNs are limited when assessing relationships between distant input features because their filters are local and built around a strong locality bias.
CNNs factorize the signal processing problem into small, local pieces that are aggregated step by step.
In a shallow CNN, the receptive field expands slowly (by one per layer), preventing a single output neuron from depending on two distant input variables.

key_terms.definition: Convolutional is a type of network where every output neuron receives input only from a local patch of the previous layer, and the weights are shared among all filters.
Locality bias is the inherent characteristic of CNNs that forces them to factorize the signal processing problem into small, local pieces.
Receptive field is the region of the original input that affects the activation of a specific neuron in a subsequent layer.
Transformer is an architecture designed to circumvent the limitations imposed by the strong locality bias found in convolutional networks.

L08.subgoal: Compare global processing methods and define the concept of sparse attention

key_points.text: Fully connected networks process data globally, but this requires $N^2$ edges and parameters, making it too compute heavy.
Attention allows for a global view of the input signal while maintaining computational efficiency by looking sparsely globally.
The core idea of attention is to focus only on the parts of the input signal that are relevant to the current problem or question.
The Transformer architecture consists of three main pieces, with attention being the second and most novel component.

key_terms.definition: Attention is an operation designed to allow a neural network to look at the entire input signal globally. This mechanism allows the network to focus only on the parts of the input that are most relevant to the current problem or question.

Fully connected network is a type of neural network where every single output neuron is connected to every input neuron. This structure allows information to be aggregated immediately and globally across the entire input.

Sparsely globally is an approach that allows a network to look at the entire input signal without requiring every neuron to be connected to every other neuron. This method maintains a global view while significantly reducing the computational load and number of parameters.

L08.subgoal: Define the concept of a token as the fundamental data unit in Transformer models

key_points.text: A token is defined as a vector of neurons, serving as an encapsulated unit of information.
Transformers operate over a set of tokens, which are vector-valued units, rather than the scalar-valued neurons used in traditional neural networks.
The concept of a token is generalized to be any chunk of information that the problem is factorized into, regardless of its specific structure.
Transformers are highly domain-agnostic, meaning the core recipe is to convert any data into a set of tokens and then apply the transformer.

key_terms.definition: Token is a vector of neurons that functions as a small, encapsulated packet or bundle of information. Token represents a fundamental unit of data that is processed within the transformer architecture.

Set of tokens is the primary data structure used to represent information in the transformer model. This set consists of multiple tokens, which are the basic units over which the transformer operates.

L08.subgoal: Explain the tokenization process and the domain-agnostic nature of transformers

key_points.text: Transformers are currently the most popular and performant deep learning method because they are agnostic to the input signal, unlike CNNs.
The general transformer strategy requires a domain expert to convert raw data into tokens, which are then processed by a generic transformer.
For images, tokenization involves breaking the image into patches and projecting each patch into a fixed-dimensional vector.
In natural language, tokens are often derived from byte pairs, which are snippets of words.
The initial tokenization step is the only part of the process that requires considering the specific input domain.

key_terms.definition: Transformer is a deep learning architecture that is currently one of the most popular and performant methods across various domains. Transformer is characterized by being agnostic to the input signal, unlike previous methods.

Tokenization is the general strategy where a domain expert converts raw data into discrete tokens that the generic transformer can process. Tokenization allows the transformer to operate on chunks of data that make sense within the specific domain.

Token is a unit of input data that is processed by the transformer, representing the input as an array of vector-valued measurements. Token is the result of projecting a set of raw measurements, such as RGB values, onto a fixed dimensional vector.
Patch is a local chunk of an image that is broken up and then converted into a token. Patch is created by chopping up the image, similar to how a Convolutional Neural Network operates.

Byte pair is a specific unit used in natural language processing that represents two byte representations of the language. Byte pair allows the system to carve up English and other natural language into manageable units.
