L08.subgoal: Define token notation and compare token vs. neuron linear combinations

key_points.text: Tokens are treated as vectors, and the resulting architectures are often permutation invariant over the ordering of these tokens.
Token-based networks utilize two fundamental operations: a linear combination and a unit-wise nonlinearity.
A linear combination of tokens is a weighted combination of vectors (rows of the token matrix T).
The token linear combination is less expressive than a neuron linear combination because it constitutes a low-rank operation.

key_terms.definition: Linear combination operation is a generalization of the linear combination that is performed over neurons. This operation is one of the two basic operations used when operating over tokens.

Linear combination of tokens is a weighted combination of vectors, where the vectors represent the tokens. This operation is represented in matrix notation by multiplying a weight matrix by the token matrix.

Permutation invariant refers to architectures that maintain the same output regardless of the ordering of the rows in the input matrix. This property is important because the ordering of tokens does not matter in these architectures.

Low rank transformation is a mathematical operation where the number of weights determining the combination is significantly smaller than the total number of individual neurons that make up the tokens. This makes the token linear combination a less expressive family of layers.

L08.subgoal: Define and explain the structure and function of token nets in transformers

key_points.text: A token-wise nonlinearity applies a function F to each token independently and identically.
The token-wise nonlinearity operation is equivalent to running a 1 by 1 convolutional filter across the sequence of tokens.
The resulting architecture, which uses vector-valued units called tokens, is referred to as a token net.
Token nets share the same fundamental motif as MLPs (linear combination followed by nonlinearity), but use vector-valued tokens instead of scalar neurons.

key_terms.definition: Token is an encapsulated unit of operations that serves as the fundamental unit in the architecture. It is a vector-valued unit, which distinguishes it from a scalar-valued neuron.
Token-wise nonlinearity is a function that operates on each token independently and identically. This nonlinearity passes every token in the array through the same nonlinear function F.
Token net is an architecture that performs a linear combination of tokens. This process involves taking a weighted sum of tokens, followed by a token-wise nonlinearity.

L08.subgoal: Compare the architectural differences and operational mechanisms of GNNs and Transformers

key_points.text: GNNs often share weights across depth, while standard Transformers typically do not share weights across depth.
In GNNs, the aggregation process is determined by the graph connectivity (adjacency matrix), unlike a Transformer which is a fully connected graph net.
Token-wise nonlinearity is typically implemented as an MLP, and its parameters are learned using backpropagation.
The fundamental concept involves operating over vector-valued units (tokens) instead of scalar-valued units (neurons).

key_terms.definition: Token is a vector-valued unit that is used in the network architecture instead of the scalar-valued units known as neurons. Operating over tokens allows the network to process complex, vector-valued information.

Unrolled GNN is a network structure that utilizes an aggregate function for weighted combination and often shares weights across its depth. This structure is equivalent to the token net version of the transformer.
Transformer is a network architecture that typically does not share weights across depth, but can. It determines the weights for aggregation through a mechanism called attention.

Graph net is a network that operates over a fully connected graph, meaning all arrows are present at every aggregation layer. It is conceptually similar to a transformer but its arrows are determined by the graph structure.
Aggregate function is the process in a GNN that performs some kind of weighted combination of input data. This function can be a linear combination or a nonlinear operation.

L08.subgoal: Explain how attention mechanisms replace fixed weights with data-driven activations

key_points.text: A standard linear combination uses a weight matrix (W) whose parameters are learned via backpropagation.
In attention, the weights used for the linear combination are not free parameters but are derived from activations elsewhere in the network.
The attention matrix (A) is determined by a function F that takes the input data being processed.
Attention allows the model to selectively focus on relevant tokens (patches) to perform tasks like counting or averaging attributes.

key_terms.definition: Attention is a mechanism that determines how a linear combination is performed between tokens, where the weights used are not fixed parameters but are derived from activations elsewhere in the network.
Transformer is a neural network architecture that utilizes the attention mechanism, allowing it to process input data by dynamically determining the weights for linear combinations.
Token is a vector of numbers that represents a descriptive part of the input data, such as a patch of an image or a word.
Linear combination is a mathematical operation where the output is calculated as a weighted sum of input tokens, which is the basis for how tokens are combined into a new representation.

Weight matrix is a matrix containing free parameters that determines the coefficients used in a linear combination, which can either be learned via backpropagation or determined by external activations.

L08.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of Query-Key-Value attention in the Transformer

key_points.text: The most common attention mechanism used is called query-key-value attention (QKV).
The relevance between a query vector and a key vector is determined by calculating their dot product.
The similarity scores are normalized using a softmax function to determine the attention weights (alpha).
The final output (T out) is a weighted combination of the Value vectors of all input tokens.

key_terms.definition: Query-key-value attention is the mathematical formulation of the most common kind of attention, which allows the transformer to map from a set of input tokens to a set of output tokens. This mechanism involves using a query to determine relevance against keys and then aggregating values.
Query is a special operation that emits a vector based on the contents of the question's embedding vector. This vector is used to determine which parts of the input signal the model should attend to.
Key is a function associated with each token that emits a vector, which the query attempts to match against. This vector represents the content of the token that the query should match to.

Value is an operation that transforms a token vector into the information that will be reported to the next layer of the network. This vector contains the actual content that is retrieved when a query matches a key.

L08.subgoal: Explain how the attention mechanism uses linear projections and the dot product to determine relevance

key_points.text: The query, key, and value vectors are linear projections of the token vector, and these projection matrices are the learnable parameters of the attention layer.
The dot product between the key vector and the query vector measures how relevant the key is to the query, indicating similarity.
The standard method for mapping the question vector to the query vector is a linear projection, though other functions are possible.
Text and images must be tokenized using separate tokenizers, as they are not tokenized the same way.

key_terms.definition: Attention layer is a concrete mechanism that utilizes three learnable matrices to transform a token vector into query, key, and value vectors. These projections constitute the learnable parameters of the attention layer.

Learnable parameters are the matrices that the model learns during training, such as the matrices that transform a token vector into a query, key, or value. These parameters are essential components of the attention layer.

Query vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to determine the relevance of other tokens. The query function maps from the question vector, which is represented by a token vector.
Key vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to be compared against a query vector. This comparison measures the similarity between the key and the query.

Dot product between the key vector and the query vector measures how relevant a specific key is to a specific query. This operation functions as a way of measuring the similarity between the two vectors.

L08.subgoal: Define self-attention and discuss its emergent properties in visual tasks

key_points.text: Self-attention allows every token in a set to emit queries to other tokens within the same signal.
Intuitively, self-attention helps a patch refine its representation by attending to and aggregating information from similar patches.
The specific attention mechanism is determined by machine learning, specifically backpropagation minimizing the objective function.
Observed behaviors, such as a horse patch attending only to other horse patches, are empirical observations and not provable rules.

key_terms.definition: Self-attention is a mechanism where every single token in a set of tokens can emit queries to all other tokens within the same signal. This allows the model to relate different parts of the input signal to each other.

L08.subgoal: Derive and explain the mathematical mechanism of self-attention

key_points.text: Self-attention determines the weights of a linear combination based on the input token sequence.
Every token in the input sequence emits a Query, Key, and Value vector via learned projection matrices (WQ, WK, WV).
The weight assigned to the linear combination is determined by the inner product (dot product) between the Query and Key vectors.
Using learned projections (Q, K, V) instead of learning the attention matrix directly reduces the number of parameters from depending on sequence length (N) to depending on dimensionality (D).

key_terms.definition: Self-attention is an idea where the weights used in a linear combination are determined as a function of the input sequence itself. This allows the model to weigh the importance of different tokens relative to each other.
Query vector is a vector emitted by every token in the input sequence via a projection (WQ) that is used to determine the attention weights. It acts as the request for information from other tokens.

Key vector is a vector emitted by every token in the input sequence via a projection (WK) that is used to calculate the dot product with the query vector. This vector serves as a label or index for the information contained in the value vector.

Value vector is a vector emitted by every token in the input sequence via a projection (WV) that holds the actual information being combined in the linear combination. The attention mechanism weights these vectors to form the output.

Attention equation is the mathematical condensation of the self-attention process, which involves multiplying the query matrix by the transpose of the key matrix. This operation calculates the similarity between all pairs of queries and keys.

L08.subgoal: Compare the parameter efficiency and structure of MLP, Convolution, and Transformer layers

key_points.text: A fully connected MLP layer has $n^2$ learnable parameters when mapping from $R^n$ to $R^n$ (647, 649).
Convolutional layers have far fewer learnable parameters than MLPs because they utilize weight sharing (656, 660).
Convolution possesses translation equivariance due to its weight sharing property (659, 660).
The Transformer attention matrix is a low-rank sparse transformation with fewer linear learnable parameters than dense layers (671, 676, 690).

key_terms.definition: Transformer is a deep learning architecture that uses a generic computational framework to process data across different modalities. It utilizes linear layers and attention mechanisms, resulting in a low-rank sparse transformation with fewer learnable parameters.

Convolution is a computational operation that uses a much lower rank matrix compared to a fully connected layer. This structure allows for far fewer learnable parameters while maintaining translation equivariance.

Attention layer is a mechanism within the Transformer that, fundamentally, operates as a linear combination of neurons. This combination allows the model to weigh the importance of different parts of the input sequence.

Translation equivariance is a property where if the input data is shifted or translated, the resulting output is translated by the same amount. This property is achieved in convolution due to weight sharing.

Low rank describes a matrix that can be represented using fewer parameters than its full dimensions would suggest. This property is advantageous because it reduces the number of linear learnable parameters in the model.

L08.subgoal: Describe the architecture and operational steps of the Vision Transformer

key_points.text: Multi-headed self-attention (MSA) uses parallel attention layers that can learn to attend to different features, such as shapes or textures.
The complete Vision Transformer architecture processes spatial signals using tokens, multi-headed self-attention (MSA), and point-wise nonlinearity (MLP).
LayerNorm is an operation that normalizes a vector to have zero mean and unit variance, which contributes to desirable optimization properties.
Residual connections allow an identity pass around the processing layers, similar to the ResNets discussed in the CNN lecture.

key_terms.definition: Residual connections involve taking an identity pass around the processing block. This technique allows the network to maintain information flow through the architecture.

L08.subgoal: Explain the necessity and implementation of positional encodings in Transformer architectures

key_points.text: Transformers are inherently permutation equivariant, meaning permuting the input sequence results in a permuted output, because their core operations (point-wise nonlinearity and attention) are order-independent.
Since many real-world tasks require the order of tokens to matter (e.g., causal impact in sentences), positional encodings are used to break the inherent permutation equivariance.
Positional encodings are typically implemented by concatenating a value to each token that indicates its location in the input signal (e.g., sentence or image).
The choice of positional encoding basis can be domain-specific; for instance, Fourier basis is used for images, while the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian is used for graphs.

key_terms.definition: Permutation equivariant means that if the input sequence of tokens is permuted, the output will also change its order accordingly. Transformers possess this property because the transformation respects the permutation of the input.

Permutation invariant means that the output remains unchanged even if the input tokens are reordered. Attention is permutation invariant because the relationship between any pair of tokens is determined solely by the values in the token vectors, not their sequence order.

Set-to-set mapping is a function where an unordered set of inputs maps to an unordered set of outputs. This characteristic implies that the ordering of the tokens does not inherently matter for the transformation.

L08.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of autoregressive language models and how GPT functions

key_points.text: Autoregressive models function by predicting the next word in a sequence (820).
The autoregressive process involves concatenating the prediction to the input sequence and continuing the prediction (821).
Language models are trained using supervised learning to classify the next word from a vocabulary (832).
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer (837).

key_terms.definition: Autoregressive model predicts the next word in a sequence by taking the previous prediction and appending it to the input sequence, then continuing the process. This model is trained to ensure its predictions match the actual text observed in the training set.
Causal attention is an extra piece that is important when mapping transformers onto language models. This mechanism is necessary for the model to process information sequentially.
Generative model is one of the kinds of models used for language and other signals. These models are designed to create new content, such as predicting the next word in a sequence.

L08.subgoal: Explain how causal masking enforces that predictions only depend on previous sequence items

key_points.text: An autoregressive transformer predicts the next item in a sequence by shifting the input and repeating the process.
For sequential generation, a prediction must only depend on previous items in the sequence, not future items.
Causal masking ensures that every output token can only attend to earlier tokens in the sequence.
The application of masking makes the transformer non-permutation equivariant, meaning the order of tokens matters.

key_terms.definition: Autoregressive transformer is a type of transformer that generates output sequentially by predicting the next item in a sequence based on previously generated items. The process involves predicting the next item, shifting the input, and repeating the cycle.

Causal masking is a technique applied to the attention matrix that ensures every output token can only attend to tokens that appeared earlier in the sequence. This operation prevents the model from looking into the future, which is necessary for generating text in time's order.

Receptive field is the set of previous words that an output token is allowed to see when predicting the next word. This field ensures that the prediction for any given word only depends on information that came before it.

L08.subgoal: Explain the Transformer architecture and its application in image-to-text tasks

key_points.text: The Transformer architecture was defined by the paper "Attention Is All You Need".
The feedforward layer applies an MLP independently and identically to every single token vector.
Cross-attention allows tokens to attend to a different set of tokens, which are not themselves.
Image-to-text captioning involves tokenizing an image and then using cross-attention to describe it.

key_terms.definition: Transformer architecture is a model defined by the paper "Attention Is All You Need" that utilizes attention mechanisms as its primary component for processing sequences.
Feedforward is the token-wise nonlinearity that involves applying a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) independently and identically to every single token vector.
Autoregressive part is a component of the model related to autoregressive modeling, where the prediction process generates outputs sequentially based on previous steps.
Positional encoding is a mechanism, often implemented using a sinusoid, that provides information about the specific position of tokens within the input sequence.
Cross-attention is a mechanism where a set of tokens attends to a different, separate set of tokens, such as text tokens attending to image tokens.

L09.subgoal: Understand the role of practical heuristics and hacks in deep learning progress

key_points.text: This lecture will focus on practical advice, heuristics, and hacks rather than formal theory.
Deep learning progress has historically been driven more by practical hacks and practitioners than by academic theory.
Classical generalization bounds, such as the VC dimension, are often vacuous and do not accurately predict the generalization ability of deep nets.
Many practical deep learning courses prioritize coding and making systems run, often treating the underlying math and theory as secondary.

key_terms.definition: Hacks are practical tips and methods that have historically driven progress in deep learning. These are often anecdotal insights from practitioners rather than formal mathematical theory.
Deep nets are neural networks that are capable of generalizing well, even when classical theoretical bounds suggest they should not.
To generalize means that a deep net can perform effectively on data that it has not encountered during the training process.
VC dimension is a classical theoretical measure used to establish generalization bounds. These bounds predict how well a system will perform based on its complexity.
Generalization bounds are theoretical limits derived from classical theories that predict how well a system will perform. These bounds can be rendered vacuous when dealing with deep nets.

L09.subgoal: Apply the principle of deep data inspection to analyze model results

key_points.text: Researchers must look at the raw data and results, rather than just relying on summary statistics or plots.
A guiding principle is to 'become friends with every pixel' or data point in your domain.
For final projects, students should show the data itself, which should be more high dimensional than a single plot.

key_terms.definition: Pixel is the fundamental unit of data, particularly in image analysis, which requires deep inspection rather than relying solely on summary statistics. Becoming friends with every pixel means thoroughly examining the raw data points in a domain.

L09.subgoal: Identify and explain the dangers of spurious correlations in deep learning

key_points.text: High accuracy in a deep net does not guarantee that it is classifying the data for the correct reason.
A model can fail by relying on a spurious correlation or shortcut, such as looking at irrelevant features outside the target tissue.
Spurious correlations often arise from data bias, where the data itself gives away the answer.
Models that rely on spurious correlations will not generalize to new environments or datasets.

key_terms.definition: Spurious correlation is a shortcut where a deep net uses an irrelevant feature, such as a marker in the corner of an image, instead of the actual tissue to make a classification.
Bias in the data occurs when the training data itself contains a systematic skew, such as only including malignant tumors from a specific hospital, which gives away the answer.
Generalize is the ability of a model to perform accurately on new, unseen data from different contexts, such as other hospitals.
Deep net is a type of neural network used in prior work to attempt to identify whether a medical scan is cancerous or not.
Imbalanced data set is a common failure scenario where the training data contains significantly more examples of one class than another, such as having 99% of cases being non-cancerous.

L09.subgoal: Understand why monitoring model outputs is crucial for debugging deep learning systems

key_points.text: Relying solely on the loss curve is superficial and does not provide a complete understanding of a model's training process.
For generative models, observing the model's outputs provides a higher-dimensional understanding of the training process than the loss function.
Model failures, such as plateauing performance, may be caused by physical issues or input problems rather than just optimization failure.
Effective debugging requires visualizing both the model's inputs and its outputs.

key_terms.definition: A generative adversarial network is a type of model that exhibits oscillatory behavior when generating images. This behavior is a characteristic feature of these models during the training process.

Reinforcement learning is a type of learning where an agent attempts to maximize a reward by interacting with an environment. The agent's goal is to achieve a desired outcome, such as chasing another entity.

L09.subgoal: Apply data inspection techniques to validate input distributions and preprocessing steps

key_points.text: Imbalanced target outputs in training data can lead to trivial results, where the model simply guesses the majority class.
When inspecting data, it is crucial to check the range, variability of units, and whether negative numbers are possible.
A common bug occurs when the assumed data format (e.g., 0 to 1) does not match the actual loaded format (e.g., 0 to 255 uint8).
Data inspection should be performed immediately before the model's forward pass to ensure the data format matches expectations.

key_terms.definition: An imbalanced set of target outputs occurs when the training data contains a disproportionate number of one class compared to others. This imbalance can lead to trivial performance metrics if the model simply guesses the majority class.

Calibration is the process of adjusting a model's predictions to reflect their true probability of correctness. This is necessary when the baseline chance of being correct is high due to data imbalance.

Data preprocessing is the necessary step of preparing raw data into the specific format required for the model to process it correctly. Failure to preprocess data can lead to significant bugs, such as incorrect range assumptions.

Random mini batches are small, randomly selected subsets of the training data used during the learning process. These batches allow the model to be trained iteratively without processing the entire dataset at once.

A prior is the initial probability or assumption about the outcome before the model has analyzed any specific input data. Naive guessing based on priors means the system predicts based solely on the overall distribution of the training data.

L09.subgoal: Understand data integrity issues and inspect tensor properties in deep learning

key_points.text: Data loading errors can occur due to library conventions, such as image flipping or channel permutation (e.g., BGR vs RGB).
A mismatch between the model's expectations and the input data format causes problems during training or inference.
Critical data properties to inspect include the data type, tensor shape, and whether the tensor requires gradients.
Statistical properties like the minimum, maximum, mean, and variance are important checks for data quality.

key_terms.definition: Tensor is a fundamental data structure in deep learning that holds numerical data, and its properties like shape and data type are critical for model operation.
Requires gradient is a property that must be set to true for any parameter that needs to be trained, allowing the network to calculate gradients during training.
Shape is the dimensional structure of tensors in deep learning, and this structure is considered super critical for the proper functioning of the network.
Data type specifies the format of the data, such as whether it is a 32-bit tensor or a uint8, which is an important characteristic to inspect.

L09.subgoal: Compare and contrast data standardization and min-max scaling techniques

key_points.text: Standardization involves subtracting the mean and dividing by the square root of the variance of the data.
Standardization makes the data invariant to the specific unit of measure used.
Min-Max scaling transforms data to lie within the range of 0 to 1.
Scaling is a good heuristic, especially for vastly different scales, to ensure gradients are not too small for smaller measurements.

key_terms.definition: Standardization transformation is a method of data normalization where the data is transformed by subtracting the mean and dividing by the square root of the variance. Standardization transformation makes the data invariant to the specific unit of measure used in the original data.

L09.subgoal: Compare how normalization techniques behave in high versus low dimensions

key_points.text: In high dimensions, things are simple, while in low dimensions, they are weird.
In high dimensions, normalization methods like RMS-norm and LayerNorm behave almost identically.
RMS-norm tends to map data points onto the unit hypersphere.
In low dimensions, the difference between normalization methods can cause a loss of degrees of freedom and data collapse.

key_terms.definition: RMS-norm is an operation that takes the Root Mean Square norm of activations, which tends to map data points onto the unit hypersphere. This operation is sometimes used to achieve good effects on learning dynamics.

Layernorm (Layer Normalization) is a standard layer used in transformers that normalizes a vector by subtracting the mean over the vector and then taking the Root Mean Square norm of the result. This operation behaves almost identically to RMS-norm in high dimensions.

High dimensions refer to spaces where the properties of data, such as a Gaussian distribution, differ significantly from human intuition derived from low-dimensional spaces. Things become simple in high dimensions, which is a key concept in deep learning.

Low dimensions refer to spaces, like the three spatial coordinates we experience, where human intuition is typically applied to understand objects and data. The lecture warns students to be careful when working in low dimensions.
Unit hypersphere is the geometric shape onto which RMS-norm tends to map data points. This mapping is the specific effect of the normalization operation.

L09.subgoal: Explain the necessity of large dimensions for stable deep learning training

key_points.text: Normalization layers like Batch Norm fail when the batch size is 1, and LayerNorm fails when the layer dimensionality is 1.
For robust deep learning, all dimensions (batch size N, M, C) should be kept large, with heuristics suggesting at least 10 or more.
As dimensions become large, deep learning behavior simplifies, leveraging the law of large numbers, similar to thermodynamics.
Although increasing scale incurs costs (time, money), larger dimensions are generally better for statistical inference and prediction.

key_terms.definition: Batch norm is a type of normalization layer that requires a sufficiently large batch size to function correctly, because taking the mean over a batch of one results in a trivial value. Batch norm is often used in deep learning to stabilize training and improve performance.

Layernorm is a type of normalization layer that requires sufficient layer dimensionality to function correctly. Layernorm is designed to prevent weird effects when the dimensionality of the layer is too small.

Asymptotically, things become simple when dealing with very large scales, similar to how thermodynamics simplifies when considering a billion atoms. This concept means that the system approaches a predictable and simple state as the scale increases indefinitely.

L09.subgoal: Apply techniques to sanity check tensor shapes and prevent data loss during casting

key_points.text: Using unique dimensions for tensor inputs helps catch errors in reshaping operations.
Casting a tensor to an unsigned integer type (like uint8) can cause negative data to be lost.
Standardizing input data often results in negative values, which cannot be represented by unsigned integer types.

key_terms.definition: A uint8 is an unsigned 8-bit integer data type that can only represent positive numbers. This limitation means that any negative data will be lost or corrupted when stored in this format.
Standardization is a process where input data is transformed to be centered on zero and have a unit variance. This transformation allows the data to contain negative values.

A tensor is a multi-dimensional data structure used in deep learning. Changing the type of a tensor (casting) must be done carefully, as it can cause negative data to be lost if the new type cannot represent it.

L09.subgoal: Introduce and demonstrate the use of einops for simplifying tensor rearrangement

key_points.text: Tensor manipulation operations like reshaping and transposing can lead to complex bookkeeping and bugs in deep learning code.
The library einops simplifies tensor operations by providing a common notation called 'rearrange'.
Einops uses a string notation to specify how dimensions map from one tensor space to another.
Einops operations often possess the property that the inverse operation returns the tensor to its original state.

key_terms.definition: Einops is a library designed to simplify complex tensor manipulation by providing a common notation for operations like reshape, flatten, and unsqueeze. This library helps make keeping track of reshape operations easier for the user.

Rearrange is a function within einops that uses a string notation to specify how a set of reshapes maps a tensor from one space to another space. This string acts as a shorthand for defining the required dimensional mapping.

Row contiguous describes the order in which a tensor is read when reshaping, meaning the operation processes the first row entirely before moving to the next row. This behavior dictates how the data is sequenced when dimensions are flattened.

An inverse operation is a sequence of operations that, when performed after an initial operation, returns the system to its original state. This property allows the original tensor to be recovered after a transformation.

L09.subgoal: Justify the use of data augmentation over designing invariant neural network architectures

key_points.text: Data augmentation increases small datasets by applying transformations that do not fundamentally change the target class.
Geometric deep learning approaches aim to design an invariant neural network architecture, whereas data augmentation forces invariance through data transformations.
Data augmentation is often preferred because it is easy, intuitive, and architecture agnostic, decoupling properties from the model design.
Domain randomization is a form of data augmentation that perturbs input training data to ensure the test data is in distribution.

L09.subgoal: Explain why increasing data difficulty improves model generalization

key_points.text: The ideal loss curve shows graceful, smooth, continual progress, indicating the problem is hard enough to learn from but not so easy that it converges too quickly.
Training on problems that converge too quickly is inefficient because it wastes optimization time (flops) in the flat region.
To improve learning, one must increase the difficulty of the data using techniques like data augmentation or domain randomization.
Making the training problem harder leads to better generalization performance.

key_terms.definition: Data augmentation is a technique that adds more data points to a dataset, which makes the learning problem more difficult for the model to solve.
Domain randomization is a method where random variation is added to the training environment to increase the difficulty of the problem, allowing the model to generalize better.
Backpropagation is the process of minimizing the loss with respect to the model's parameters, which is the main optimization task in deep learning.
Loss curve is a visual representation of training progress that shows how the model's loss changes over time during an experiment.
Generalization is the ability of a trained model to perform well on new test environments or data that it has not seen during the training process.

L09.subgoal: Explain how data randomization improves generalization and why data is critical in practice

key_points.text: Adding randomization makes the problem harder, forcing the model to generalize better to real-world test cases, even if it takes longer to train.
High training accuracy often indicates that the problem is too easy and needs to be made harder to generalize better.
In real-world industry scenarios, changing the data is often more impactful than changing the learning algorithm.
Companies can gain leverage by collecting more data, collecting better data, or labeling data in new ways.

key_terms.definition: Domain randomization is a technique used to minimize the gap between a source domain, such as a simulation, and a target domain, such as reality. This is achieved by introducing random variations into the source domain during training.

Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on test cases, which are the real-world cases, rather than just performing well on the training cases. Making the problem sufficiently hard is necessary to achieve better generalization.

Robustness is the quality of a model that allows it to maintain performance even when facing variations or errors in the input data. By training with randomized inputs, the model becomes robust to potential miscalibrations or errors.

Data is the primary variable that can be changed in real-world industry scenarios, unlike the fixed data typically used in academic research. Changing the data is considered a highly leveraged tool for improving machine learning outcomes.

L09.subgoal: Demonstrate how increasing input information simplifies prediction problems using examples

key_points.text: Prediction becomes easier the longer the input, because more information is available for the prediction.
Historically, early NLP models (N-grams) often limited the input size (N) unnecessarily.
The more information you condition on, the easier the prediction problem becomes.
To improve predictive performance in real-world scenarios, one should add diverse information to the input features (X).

key_terms.definition: Language model is a system that attempts to predict the next word in a sequence of sentences. This model is used to understand the structure and probability of language.
N-gram model is a statistical model that represents how words co-occur with each other in a sequence. These models are used to estimate the probability of word sequences.

Joint distribution is the statistical measure that the N-gram error models, representing the probability of all elements occurring together. This distribution considers the entire sequence of words simultaneously.

Conditional distribution is the statistical measure that the current model is designed to model, specifically the probability of the last word given the preceding words. This focuses on predicting the next element based on the input history.

L09.subgoal: Explain how high-dimensional input reduces uncertainty in deep learning models

key_points.text: Standard neural networks typically model point predictions (like regression) and do not handle complex output distributions of possibilities.
A key technique is to provide enough information in the input (X) so that the probability of the output (Y) becomes deterministic, acting like a delta function.
Modern text-to-image models succeed because they use rich input (like sentences) to make the data problem almost deterministic, allowing standard neural net methods to work.
To improve models, it is recommended to make the data big (more samples) and make the input (X) a big, high-dimensional vector.

key_terms.definition: Generative models are types of models that handle uncertainty by modeling the entire possible space of data, rather than just predicting a single output value.
Delta function is a mathematical representation of a single point, which occurs when the probability of an output becomes completely deterministic.
Simple Gaussian distribution is a type of distribution that is used when modeling complicated distributions, provided that the model is conditioned on a large amount of information.
Regression is a task where standard neural net training uses functions like L2 loss to take inputs and make a single point prediction of the output value.

L09.subgoal: Explain the importance of data diversity and model simplicity in machine learning

key_points.text: When the target event in data is extremely rare, simply scaling up the data is inefficient because most of the data represents the common, well-understood case.
To improve performance in rare event detection, adding context or more information into the input data is a key strategy.
The first principle of modeling is to keep models simple, as simplicity makes them easier to understand, debug, and allows for theoretical guarantees.
Simple models are often the most powerful because the simplest model that fits the data is generally the best, following Occam's razor.
Researchers should prioritize simplicity over adding complexity just to achieve a marginal increase in accuracy on benchmarks.

key_terms.definition: Distribution shift is a problem that occurs when the data used for training differs from the data encountered in the real world. This issue becomes critical when scaling data, especially when dealing with extremely rare events.

Data diversity and coverage is the key factor that matters when dealing with rare classes of interest. This concept suggests that the data must adequately represent all the different things that are important in the domain.

Context is additional information added into the inputs of a model to provide surrounding circumstances. By knowing the context, a model can adjust its probability of certain states, such as reducing the probability of a crash if the context is an amusement park.

Occam's razor is an intuitive argument used to support the idea that the simplest model that fits the data will be the best model. This principle suggests that complexity should be avoided unless absolutely necessary.

L09.subgoal: Apply practical heuristics for selecting robust and useful deep learning models

key_points.text: For practical systems, simplicity and popularity often matter more than raw performance.
GitHub stars are a better proxy for a model's usefulness than its accuracy on a leaderboard.
Training models on diverse or out-of-domain data is a beneficial principle.
For practical purposes, it is generally advised to use pre-trained models rather than training from scratch.

key_terms.definition: Pre-training is the practice of training a model on a wide variety of data, including related datasets, even if the final problem only concerns a specific dataset. This principle suggests that training on as much information as possible is generally beneficial.

Pre-trained model is a model that has already been trained on large amounts of data, and for practical purposes, students should start with these existing models rather than training systems from scratch. This advice is crucial for getting a system to work efficiently.
Transfer learning is a concept related to pre-training, which involves leveraging knowledge gained from one task or dataset to improve performance on a different, related task.
Out-of-domain data is data that is not specific to the problem being solved, and using it in the training set is beneficial because it helps put as much information into the model as possible.

State of the art model refers to the latest and greatest models in a field, which are typically tracked on leaderboards to measure peak performance. However, for practical application, popularity often matters more than this peak performance.

L09.subgoal: Explain how to reduce image colorization to classification and justify the theoretical benefits

key_points.text: Transforming a complex problem into a known, solved problem (reducibility) helps in understanding the original problem.-
Colorization can be converted into classification by quantizing the continuous color space into discrete classes.-
A ConvNet used with a sliding window operator allows for per-pixel classification across an image.-
Classification using softmax is more expressive than regression because it models a fully expressive distribution over discrete variables.-

key_terms.definition: Empirical risk minimization is a method used to find a function that makes correct predictions on the training data and expectation. This process aims to minimize the difference between the predicted outcomes and the actual outcomes.
Quantize is the process of reducing a continuous space into discrete classes. This allows continuous values, such as colors, to be represented by distinct, countable categories.

Softmax regression is a method used to formulate a problem as classification, often utilizing the softmax cross-entropy loss. This technique allows the model to predict a probability distribution over discrete classes.

Softmax distribution is a fully expressive categorical distribution that models a probability mass function over a discrete vocabulary. This distribution is the most general way of quantifying uncertainty over a discrete variable.

One-hot vector is a representation used to label discrete classes, similar to how labels are used in standard classification problems. Each class is represented by a vector where only one element is active.

L09.subgoal: Identify best practices and common pitfalls when designing and training deep learning models

key_points.text: A basic deep learning recipe involves transforming data into one-hot vectors and using cross-entropy classification with Adam and Transformer.
Batch normalization is discouraged because it creates a strong dependency on batch size and causes performance differences between training and testing.
Layer normalization is the current standard alternative to batch normalization.
Model performance can be improved by scaling up data, increasing model size, or training the model for a longer duration.

key_terms.definition: Batch normalization is a technique that normalizes activations using the statistics derived from a specific data batch. This process introduces a strong dependency between the model's performance and the batch size.

Layer norm is the current standard technique for normalizing activations, which is recommended as an alternative to batch normalization. Layer norm is used to avoid the performance issues associated with batch size changes.

One-hot vector is a method used to transform data, typically categorical data, into a numerical format suitable for deep learning models. This transformation is a good default choice when starting a new deep learning domain.

Cross-entropy classification is a method used to transform the learning goal of a problem into a classification task suitable for deep learning. This transformation is a recommended default choice for setting up a deep learning problem.

Batch size is a cardinal hyperparameter in deep learning that dictates how many data points are processed simultaneously during training. Batch normalization introduces a strong dependency on this parameter, which can complicate model tuning.

L09.subgoal: Apply best practices for model development and interpret deep learning loss metrics

key_points.text: Scaling is a necessary condition for achieving human-like intelligence, but it is not sufficient on its own.
Model refinement should follow an 'add, remove, remove' process until the system stops working.
When optimizing models, the process should start by overfitting to a single data point before scaling up.
In binary classification, a loss of -0.69 indicates that the model is performing at chance level.
Students should use coding assistants for learning, but must always prioritize their own thinking and understanding.

key_terms.definition: Log probabilities are numbers frequently used in deep learning, often related to the probabilities of data under a model. These values are typically negative, and their magnitude must be interpreted carefully when evaluating model performance.

Cross-entropy loss is a measure of performance in deep learning that represents the average log probability of the data under the model. This loss function is commonly used in classification problems.

Regression loss is a type of loss function used when predicting continuous values, such as least-squares loss. Unlike log likelihood, the minimizer for regression loss is typically zero, meaning negative values indicate a potential bug.

L09.subgoal: Understand how EMA smooths training and why deep learning design requires combining techniques

key_points.text: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smooths values by mixing new values with previous values multiplied by a decay factor.
EMA allows replacing averaging across space (batch dimension) with averaging across time (iterates) in training.
There is no single best solution in deep learning; the optimal model requires finding the right combination of techniques.
Different components in a model serve various functions, such as regularization, increasing capacity, or speeding up optimization.

key_terms.definition: Exponentially Moving Average is a technique used to smooth out values over time. This method mixes a new value with previous values, where the contribution of older values is exponentially decayed by a specific factor.

Regularization refers to the addition of components to a model that have a specific effect on its performance. These components are necessary because every added regularizer influences the model and helps solve the problem.

Skip connection is a structural element that is necessary when dealing with a very deep architecture. The need for this connection may be mitigated if the model uses an optimizer that prevents vanishing gradients.

L10.subgoal: Motivate the need for sequence modeling in complex scene understanding

key_points.text: The new class of architectures being introduced is Turing complete, representing a general framework for handling memory and sequences.
Computer vision models can identify objects and attributes from a single frame.
Understanding complex relationships, predicting future actions, and grasping human intent requires temporal context and sequence information.
The lecture will introduce Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) to model sequences.

key_terms.definition: Sequence modeling is the process of modeling data that possesses an inherent order or temporal structure, such as time or order. This approach allows models to handle information that unfolds over a series of steps.

Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is a type of neural network designed to process sequences by having internal connections that allow information from previous steps to influence the current output. This structure enables the network to maintain a form of memory across the sequence.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a specific subset of Recurrent Neural Networks that is designed to overcome the common issue of forgetting information over long sequences. It achieves this by managing the flow of information within the network.

Turing complete is a property of a computational framework that signifies it is the most general type of architecture. This means the framework can theoretically perform any computation that a Turing machine can.

Autoregression is a method of modeling sequences where the prediction of a future value is based on the values that came before it in the sequence. This technique relies on the historical data within the sequence to make future predictions.

L10.subgoal: Explain how convolutional networks can model temporal data and perform convolutions in time

key_points.text: Sequences can represent various data types, including language, audio, and video.
CNNs can be extended into a 4D space-time cube, treating time as another spatial dimension.
Temporal structure can be modeled by taking slices (horizontal or vertical) through the space-time cube.
Convolutions in time function as sequence-to-sequence models and are not constrained by the structure of an image.

key_terms.definition: Sequence is an ordered collection of data points that can represent various types of information. These sequences include words in language, pictures in a video, or audio signals.

Space-time cube is a four-dimensional tensor created by extending convolutional neural networks (CNNs) into the space-time dimension. This structure allows for the representation of data that includes spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension.

Convolutions in time are a method where a weight matrix is learned over a fixed time window, similar to standard convolutions. This allows the model to process sequences by taking input from multiple positions in the sequence and generating an output position.

L10.subgoal: Explain the limitations of fixed-window convolutions and the motivation for memory units

key_points.text: As time sequences become arbitrarily long, standard convolutional approaches struggle to maintain memory of events that occurred at the beginning of the sequence.
Fixed time windows in a convolutional approach only provide local information and do not inherently contain inputs from the beginning of the sequence.
To overcome the limitations of fixed windows, models must capture context and be able to remember what was seen in the past.
The need to identify objects based on context from past observations is the primary motivation behind the development of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

key_terms.definition: Temporal convolution is a type of convolution that processes input data across a time dimension, utilizing the same weight matrix across the entire sequence.
Memory unit is a component that provides context by storing and giving information about what has been seen in the past of a sequence.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a type of network developed to capture context by remembering information from the past of a sequence.

L10.subgoal: Define the structure and mathematical components of a recurrent neural network

key_points.text: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) overcome the fixed window limitation of models like CNNs and Transformers by allowing infinite context through memory.
The core mechanism of an RNN involves using a hidden unit to take the current input and the memory from the past to predict the output and update the memory.
The functions that govern the hidden state and the output prediction are shared across all time steps.
Because of the feedback loop from the hidden state to itself, RNNs are not a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
The new hidden state is calculated by applying a non-linearity to the previous hidden state and the current input data.

key_terms.definition: A recurrent neural network is a type of network that makes the context window infinite, allowing it to process sequences of arbitrary length. This structure enables the network to maintain memory across time steps.
A hidden unit is a mechanism that takes the current input and the previous hidden state to predict the output. This unit also carries memory forward in time to the next time step.

A Directed Acyclic Graph is a graph structure where information flows strictly forward without any loops or cycles. The presence of a cycle, as in a recurrent network, means the structure is not a DAG.

L10.subgoal: Analyze the mechanism and limitations of recurrent neural network memory

key_points.text: Recurrent architectures extend scalar operations to multi-dimensional tensors, allowing for complex state representation.,
The hidden state is intended to capture the most relevant historical information from the input sequence.
Although the hidden state depends only on the previous state, the architecture recursively captures information from all prior states.,,
The current RNN construction makes it difficult to learn across very long time horizons due to limited capacity and mathematical limitations.,

key_terms.definition: Hidden state is a component of the network designed to capture the most relevant historical information from previous inputs. This state allows the network to maintain a memory of past data points.

Recurrence is the process where information is sent forward over time, allowing the network to process sequential data. This mechanism enables the network to depend on previous states to determine the current state.

Deep recurrent neural network is an architecture that stacks multiple hidden layers, allowing for many different hidden states to process sequential data. This structure extends the basic recurrent unit by adding depth.

Backprop is the process of calculating gradients for learning, which becomes complicated when the network structure does not have a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). This challenge arises because the recurrent nature of the network creates dependencies across time steps.

L10.subgoal: Explain how backpropagation is applied to networks with loops by truncating the time window

key_points.text: Backpropagation is intended for feedforward networks (DAGs), but recurrent networks contain loops.
To apply backprop to a network with loops, the network is unrolled over a fixed time window, which converts it into a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
Truncating the time window limits the model's ability to learn information from very far back in time.
The size of the fixed time window is a hyperparameter that can be tuned or informed by domain knowledge.

key_terms.definition: Backpropagation is the method used to calculate gradients during training, which is traditionally intended for feedforward networks. It allows the network to learn by propagating error signals backward through the structure.

Fixed time window is a predetermined duration during training that the model is configured to propagate back through. This window allows the recurrent network to be unrolled into a structure suitable for backpropagation.
Unroll is the process of expanding a recurrent network over a specific time window. This process transforms the network, which originally contained loops, into a directed acyclic graph.

A Directed acyclic graph is a graph structure where all nodes are connected but there are no loops. This structure is necessary because it allows standard backpropagation to be applied to networks with recurrent connections.

L10.subgoal: Explain backpropagation through shared parameters in sequence models

key_points.text: When unrolling a sequence model, the weights (W's) that map hidden states forward through time are shared across all time steps.
Backpropagation over shared parameters is equivalent to calculating gradients over a branching structure in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
When calculating the gradient for a shared parameter, the gradients from every instance where that parameter occurs must be summed up.
In frameworks like PyTorch, autograd handles the summing of gradients automatically, provided that deep copies of variables are avoided.

key_terms.definition: Gradient descent is the method used to optimize a model by learning how to change parameters (W, U, and V) so that the sum of the loss over a sequence is minimized.

A directed acyclic graph is a structure that models shared parameters, where the branching structure allows the gradient calculation to be simplified. When taking the gradient over this structure, the gradients for a parameter are summed each time it occurs.

L10.subgoal: Analyze how recurrence leads to vanishing and exploding gradients in RNNs

key_points.text: RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because the required memory size grows non-parametrically with the sequence length.
The recurrence relationship causes the weight matrix to be raised to the power of the time step (W^N).
This exponential relationship leads to vanishing gradients (small weights go to 0) or exploding gradients (large weights go to infinity).
Vanishing gradients correspond to old memories being forgotten, while exploding gradients correspond to unstable training.

key_terms.definition: Markov assumption is a principle stating that the future hidden state only depends on the immediate preceding hidden state. This assumption is used by Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to simplify dependency modeling.
Recurrent describes a model where the hidden state depends only on the immediate hidden state from the previous step. This structure allows the model to process sequences of data.
Vanishing gradients occur when the gradients become extremely small during training. This issue often results in old observations being forgotten by the network.
Exploding gradients occur when the gradients become extremely large during training. This condition leads to unstable training and is undesirable for model performance.

L10.subgoal: Explain the mechanism and components of LSTM memory control

key_points.text: LSTMs were introduced to address the vanishing gradient problem inherent in standard RNNs.
LSTMs utilize a cell state (C), which functions like a memory tape, to store information that is modulated by internal gates.
The forget and input gates use sigmoid functions, which are bounded between 0 and 1, to explicitly control what information is retained or added to the cell state.
The gating functionality and the default identity update prevent the exponential growth or decay of gradients, mitigating vanishing and exploding gradient issues.

key_terms.definition: Cell state is a new component introduced in an LSTM that functions like the hidden tape in a Turing machine. This state is modulated by the mechanisms that decide what information to forget and what information to add.

Gating functionality is the mechanism provided by multiplicative updates to the cell state, allowing the model to explicitly learn what information to remember and what information to forget. This functionality is provided by components that decide what to save and what to delete.
Sigmoid function is a non-linearity used in the LSTM that is bounded between 0 and 1. This bounding allows the function to map large values to 1 and small values to 0.

Identity is the default behavior of the LSTM, which is similar to a skipped or residual connection in a ResNet. This allows the model to potentially learn to simply send the same information forward without modification.

L10.subgoal: Describe the mechanism of autoregressive sequence generation and next-word classification

key_points.text: Autoregressive models predict the next element in a sequence and feed that prediction back into the input for the subsequent prediction (,).
The probability of a sequence is modeled by factorizing the joint distribution into a product of conditional probabilities (,).
Next-word prediction can be treated as a multi-class classification problem using a softmax function (,).
To manage large vocabularies, an alternative is to represent every character as a class, though this increases the number of time steps (,).

key_terms.definition: Autoregressive model is a type of sequence model where the system predicts the next element in a sequence based on the elements that came before it. The prediction made at one time step is then fed back into the model as input for predicting the subsequent element.
Conditional distribution is the probability of a specific next word given all the preceding words in a sequence. This concept is used to factorize the probability of an entire sequence.
Softmax is a function that takes an input and transforms it into a probability distribution. This function ensures that the outputs are non-negative and sum up to one.

Next-word classifier is a model designed to predict the most likely word that follows a given sequence of words. This model treats the sequence prediction task as a multi-class classification problem.

L10.subgoal: Compare autoregressive generation methods with memory-based and attention architectures

key_points.text: During training, teacher forcing is often used in sequence generation to condition each next word prediction on the ground-truth preceding words, rather than the model's own prediction.
Beam search is an algorithm used in autoregressive modeling to explore multiple likely paths (top k) and select the sequence with the highest overall probability.
Modern language modeling often utilizes Transformers, which allow for sharing information across all time steps simultaneously, instead of relying solely on sequential models.
Memory networks allow every time step to maintain a memory unit, enabling direct linking of old memories to future predictions without constrained sequential passing.

key_terms.definition: Byte pairs are a tokenization method that represents words using pairs of characters. These tokens are frequently used even in the largest scale language models.

Teacher forcing is a training technique where the model is conditioned on the ground-truth preceding words, even if the model predicts an incorrect word at a given time step. This prevents the model from penalizing itself for mistakes made after the initial error.

Autoregressive modeling is a process where the model predicts the next element in a sequence one step at a time. This prediction is conditioned on the previous elements that have already been generated.

Beam search is a decoding technique that allows the model to choose the top k most likely candidates at each step. It fills out a tree of possibilities and selects the path that scores best overall, representing the model's confidence in the entire sequence.

A memory unit is a concept where every single time step is allowed to maintain a memory representation. This allows for direct linking of old memories to future predictions, rather than strictly passing information forward in a constrained way.

L10.subgoal: Compare sequence modeling architectures and explain methods for scaling context windows

key_points.text: Standard self-attention has a quadratic computational complexity ($O(N^2)$) with respect to sequence length $N$.
Sparsification methods, such as Reformer and Performer, reduce attention complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$ or $O(N \log N)$ using low-rank approximation.
Longformer and Transformer XL increase context windows by deconstructing attention into local and global attention.
Retrieval-enhanced transformers use external knowledge bases to enforce factual validity and prevent hallucinations.

key_terms.definition: Recurrence is a method for modeling arbitrarily long sequences where recurrent weights are shared over time, passing forward information across a time window. This process can be implemented using vanilla recursion or more complex structures like an LSTM.

Convolution is a method for modeling arbitrarily long sequences using a fixed set of convolution weights that are shared over time. However, this method cannot see anything outside of the defined time window of that convolution.

Attention is a mechanism where weights are dynamically determined as a function of the data, which makes the way information is kept dependent on the inputs. This flexibility allows for highly adaptable sequence modeling.
Self-attention is a computation where the similarity of the entire sequence is calculated against itself. This process requires an $N^2$ computation, where $N$ is the length of the sequence.

Retrieval enhanced transformers is an architecture that decomposes a large language model into a lightweight language model and a memory bank. This setup allows the model to perform fact lookup in a database, helping to enforce factual validity.

L10.subgoal: Evaluate the practical necessity and limitations of long-term context in AI models

key_points.text: Context windows have scaled significantly, with models reaching up to 100K tokens (Q671, Q673).
Many video action recognition benchmarks only require short temporal context, such as two seconds (Q686, Q687).
The benchmarks used in machine learning directly influence the types of progress researchers prioritize (Q692).
Training and running models with large context windows requires significant power, energy, and time (Q678, Q679).

key_terms.definition: Context window is the maximum number of tokens or data points that a model can consider or process at one time. This limit determines how far back in the input sequence a model can look when generating output.

Minimum certificate set is the smallest total amount of frames or clips of a video that is required to accurately recognize a specific action. This concept helps determine the necessary temporal scope for a task.

Activations are the statistical data points that are generated when input data is passed through a frozen neural network. These statistics represent the state of the data as it moves through the network.

Temporal information refers to the time-based data or sequence of events within a video that is necessary for recognizing an action. This information allows a model to understand how events unfold over time.

L10.subgoal: Understand weights and activations as representations of fast or slow memory

key_points.text: Network parameters (theta) can be viewed as slow memory, representing statistics of the entire training data set.
Activations can be viewed as fast memory, representing statistics or memory of a single existing data point.
Hypernets, which output weights of other networks, function as a form of fast memory for the input data.
Codebooks utilize learned tensors of activations, suggesting that activations can also function as slow memory of the dataset.

key_terms.definition: Parameter represents some statistics of the training data, acting as a form of slow memory of the entire training dataset. These values are built up slowly as the network is trained.

Activation represents some statistics or memory of an existing data point, functioning as a form of fast memory within the network. This memory is related to the data currently running through the network.
Hypernet is a type of network that outputs the weights of other networks. These networks are used as a version of neural architecture search.
Codebook uses tensors of activations that are learned. This allows backpropagation to be performed directly onto the activations themselves.

L11.subgoal: Define representation learning and its relationship to neural network encoding

key_points.text: Representation learning is a new perspective on deep learning associated with generative modeling.
Deep neural networks transform raw data layer by layer into increasingly abstract representations, called embeddings.
The forward direction through a neural network is called the encoding direction, which is where representation learning operates.
The backward direction, which goes from abstract representations back to data, is called generative modeling.

key_terms.definition: Representation is the transformed version of data that is produced by a neural network. Each layer within the deep net holds a representation of the input data.
Encoding direction is the forward process through a neural network. This direction transforms raw data into simpler, more abstract representations.

Generative modeling is the process that moves from abstract representations and latent variables back toward the original data. This process is considered the inverse of the forward direction in a neural network.
Representation learning is the process that operates in the encoding direction of a neural network. It aims to find an effective mapping from raw data to useful embeddings.

L11.subgoal: Explain how data is mapped to simpler, lower-dimensional representations using encoders

key_points.text: X2vec is a method for converting input data (X) into vector representations, which is also known as feature extraction.
Neural network representations are vectors or tensors of neural activations that can represent semantic concepts like 'car' or 'ground'.
An encoder is the mapping that transforms high-dimensional data distributions into simpler, often Gaussian, lower-dimensional representations.
Functions can be represented as a mapping between sets of points in the input dimension and the set of points in the output dimension.

key_terms.definition: Data to vector (X2vec) is a method for transforming input data (X) into vector representations. People have developed this technique to apply across various data modalities.

Representation is the vector or tensor of neural activations that describes the input data at a specific layer of neural processing. These representations may indicate semantic concepts such as a car or a building.
Encoder is the mapping function that transforms data into a representation. This mapping is used to move from the original data space to the representation space.

Manifold is a high-dimensional, complicated object, such as the space of images, that is often mapped to a simpler structure. The representation space is frequently a simpler object than the original data manifold.

L11.subgoal: Explain how basic neural network layers perform geometric transformations on data

key_points.text: Linear layers perform affine transformations, which geometrically look like rotating, squishing, or scaling the input data.
The ReLU function maps all data in the negative half-space to zero, resulting in a sparse representation.
Layers using L2 norm map data to unitary vectors, meaning the vectors have a norm of 1 and lie on a hypersphere.
The output of a softmax function is a point in the simplex, which is the set of points where the dimensions sum to 1.

key_terms.definition: Linear layer takes input data and performs an affine transformation, which geometrically appears as rotating, squishing, or scaling the input data. This transformation is a geometric manipulation of the input data.
Softmax is a function that maps input data to a point within the simplex. The output of Softmax represents the probability of belonging to different classes.
Simplex is the set of points in R^d where the dimensions of those points sum up to 1. The output of a Softmax function is always a point in the simplex.
L2 norm is a function that takes all data and maps it to unitary vectors. Unitary vectors are vectors that possess a norm of 1.

L11.subgoal: Illustrate how an MLP transforms data representations for non-linear classification

key_points.text: The example uses a three-layer MLP to perform binary classification on non-linearly separable data (red cloud vs. blue hemisphere).
During training, the representation of the data distribution is transformed layer by layer.
The optimization process successfully segregates the two classes, moving the red and blue points apart.
Each layer of the network provides a progressively better representation for solving the classification task.

key_terms.definition: Binary classification is a task where the goal is to categorize input data into one of two distinct classes. In this example, the task involves separating red points from blue points.

A Non-linear classification problem is a scenario where no single linear hyperplane can successfully separate the different classes of data. This requires a more complex transformation to achieve separation.

Representation is the transformation of the data distribution that occurs layer by layer within the network. Each layer provides a progressively better representation for solving the specific classification task.
Softmax regression is a method used for classification that clamps the output values onto a simplex. This process allows the network to output probabilities for each class.

L11.subgoal: Illustrate how deep networks transform entangled input into separated semantic representations

key_points.text: Different optimization schemes (like SGD vs. Spectral Descent) perform differently, affecting the dynamics and final loss of a model.
The initial layers of a network may perform orthogonal transformations, such as rotations and scaling.
Deep networks gradually transform entangled input data into cleanly separated semantic representations layer by layer.
Networks trained for classification progressively disentangle features (classes) as they move deeper into the architecture.

key_terms.definition: Representation learning is the process of transforming entangled and complicated input data, such as images, into a neural network's internal feature space. This process gradually morphs and disentangles the data layer by layer until the semantics of interest are cleanly separated.

Spectral descent method is an optimization scheme that normalizes the updates by their spectral norm. This method is compared to standard gradient descent to observe different dynamics in loss reduction.

Dimensionality reduction technique (PCA) is a method used to visualize high-dimensional embeddings by projecting them into a lower-dimensional space. This technique is used here to show what the features extracted by the network look like.

Classification is a task where a network is trained to find a way to disentangle different classes of data. The network's representation is separated in a high-dimensional space so that a final softmax operation can predict the correct class.

L11.subgoal: Compare how human visual systems and deep neural networks learn hierarchical representations

key_points.text: The structure of the human visual cortex, which processes information through sequential layers, served as an initial inspiration for deep learning architectures.
In both the brain and deep nets, initial layers detect simple features like edges, which combine into complex patterns in deeper layers.
Researchers use interpretability methods to probe deep nets, measuring neuron responses to determine what specific inputs they are responsive to.
Deep networks successfully develop a hierarchical structure, moving from simple features to complex object recognition, such as faces, in deeper layers.

key_terms.definition: Representation learning is the process of training neural networks to learn internal representations of data, such as images, that can be used for specific tasks like classification. This process aims to understand what the neural networks are learning internally.

Mechanistic interpretability is a modern name for the type of work that involves probing and interpreting the representations learned within deep neural networks. This field seeks to understand what the emergent detectors are within these complex systems.

A filter is a component within a convolutional network that attempts to find a specific feature in the data and discard everything else. It is designed to respond selectively to certain things, such as edges or colors.
A feature map is the output generated by a filter, which is a spatially varying set of activations. It shows where the filter was most strongly activated within the input image.

A pattern detector is a neuron or filter in a deep network that becomes selectively responsive to increasingly complex patterns as the network progresses through more layers. These detectors range from simple edges to complex objects like faces.

L11.subgoal: Explain the role of learned representations in accelerating future learning via transfer learning

key_points.text: A representation of a data domain is defined as an encoder function that maps data from that domain into vector embeddings in Rd.
The main purpose of learning representations is to accelerate future learning by making subsequent tasks easier.
The transfer learning paradigm involves pre-training a network on massive data to learn a good representation, and then adapting that representation to a new task using little data.
Adaptation can be achieved by freezing the pre-trained encoder and training only a final readout (linear probe), or by fine-tuning the entire network.

key_terms.definition: Representation is a vector embedding or a more general tensor object used to map data. It can refer to the function that maps a data domain to embeddings, or it can refer to the specific vector embedding of a single data point.
Encoder is a function that maps data from a specific domain or distribution into vector embeddings in R^d. This function assigns a feature vector to every element in the input domain.
Learned representation is the set of weights and biases that parameterize the encoder function. This set of parameters constitutes the learned representation of the data distribution.
