Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on the true distribution. This is guaranteed if the new distribution where the model is used is within a certain distance of the true distribution.

L17.subgoal: Explain how Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses class imbalance and fairness

key_points.text: Standard models may ignore minority subgroups, resulting in low overall error even if the minority group's accuracy is poor.-
DRO automatically reweights data to force the model to pay more attention to minority classes.
DRO works by placing less emphasis on noisy features and shifting the distribution to make classes more separable.-
DRO is applied to fairness problems to prevent models from being biased against specific demographic groups.-

key_terms.definition: Class imbalance challenges occur when a dataset has a disproportionate number of examples in one category. This can cause a model to ignore minority groups and still achieve a decent overall loss.

L17.subgoal: Describe various strategies for improving model generalization against distribution shifts

key_points.text: One approach to distribution shift is using distributionally robust optimization or building extensions to make models more robust or fair.
Models can explicitly learn priors over distribution shifts, such as using spatiotemporal priors to remap likelihoods in species identification.
Domain adaptation is a category of models that aligns representations between a source and target domain to enforce generalization, even with limited target data.

key_terms.definition: Distribution shift is the phenomenon where the data distribution used during training differs from the distribution of the data encountered during deployment. This shift is a primary challenge when trying to ensure model generalization.

Distributionally robust optimization is an algorithmic approach designed to make models more robust against various types of distribution shifts. It aims to reduce the impact of these shifts during model training.
Subpopulation shift is a specific type of distribution shift where the data distribution changes across different subpopulations. This requires specialized methods to account for these variations.

Domain adaptation is a category of models that learns to align representations between a source domain and a target domain. This allows the model to generalize or adapt to a new target domain even if there is limited labeled data.

L17.subgoal: Evaluate the practical strategies for improving model robustness and generalization

key_points.text: Model failure modes can be diagnosed by breaking down evaluation across different dimensions, such as participant sex or time of day.
The most effective way to make a model robust is to use training data that is representative of the test domain.
If large-scale training data cannot be collected due to constraints (e.g., endangered species or deep sea environments), human review of the data is often required.
When time and effort are limited, labeling more data is often the most practical solution for improving model performance.

key_terms.definition: Failure mode refers to the specific ways a model performs poorly, which can be diagnosed to reveal underlying biases present in the initial training data.
Counterfactuals are hypothetical scenarios generated by AI models that are used to help diagnose or understand a model's failure modes.
Fairness is a concept evaluated by breaking down performance across different dimensions, such as sex or time of day, to examine relative performance across categories.
In-distribution training data is the type of data that is representative of the domain where the model is expected to operate successfully.
Generative AI models are modern artificial intelligence systems used to create hypothetical counterfactuals to aid in the diagnosis of model failure modes.

L17.subgoal: Discuss the trade-offs between generalizable robustness and targeted distribution adaptation

key_points.text: Out-of-distribution generalization is a significant challenge that helps researchers understand neural network learning and data usage limitations.
The choice of activation functions (e.g., ReLU or GELU) is a topic of research regarding its effect on model generalization or robustness.
Generalizable robustness aims to be robust to any hypothetical change, whereas adaptation optimizes performance for a specific, known distribution shift.
Methods like Reinforcement Learning or Direct Preference Optimization can be more efficient than robust training when targeting a specific dataset.

key_terms.definition: Out-of-distribution generalization is the challenge of ensuring a model performs well when encountering data that differs from the data it was trained on. Digging into this challenge helps researchers understand what neural networks learn and how training data relates to effective model usage.

Distribution shifts refer to changes in the underlying data distribution between the training phase and the deployment phase. This concept helps distinguish between being robust to general shifts versus adapting to a specific shift.
Adversarial examples are specific inputs that are designed to fool a neural network model. These examples demonstrate the vulnerability of models to subtle perturbations in the data.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a method where an agent learns optimal behavior by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback. This approach can be more cost-saving than example-by-example robust training when dealing with noise.

Domain adaptation is a technique used to improve model performance when applying a model trained on one data domain to a different, related data domain. This method is one way to address the problem of distribution shifts.

L18.subgoal: Outline the different methods and topics covered in the transfer learning mini-series

key_points.text: The core idea of transfer learning is to learn effectively even when limited data is available.
Transfer learning methods include fine-tuning, domain adaptation, and knowledge distillation.
Deep learning algorithms do not saturate with data like older learning algorithms.
Current machine learning models have far more capacity than the amount of available data.

key_terms.definition: Transfer learning is the high-level idea of trying to learn even when very little data is available by applying knowledge learned from one model to a new task or distribution.
Knowledge distillation is a method used for transferring knowledge specifically about the outputs of a machine learning model.
Foundation models represent a new paradigm in transfer learning, which introduces concepts like in-context learning and prompting.
In-context learning is a mechanism for transfer learning that involves simply asking the model a question or providing context to facilitate knowledge transfer.
Prompting is a mechanism for transfer learning that involves asking the model a question to transfer knowledge.

L18.subgoal: Apply few-shot learning concepts to understand pattern recognition challenges

key_points.text: Few-shot learning is the idea that learning can occur even when very little data is available.
Humans are highly effective at recognizing patterns and applying them to novel situations.
A challenge in few-shot learning is that limited data can lead to ambiguity regarding category boundaries.
Providing more diverse examples helps clarify the boundaries of the concept being learned.
Traditional deep learning typically begins with a dataset and an empty slate.

key_terms.definition: Few-shot learning is the idea that a model can learn to recognize similarity and patterns even when provided with very little data. This allows the model to generalize from limited examples and past experience.

L18.subgoal: Explain the motivation and mechanism of transfer learning

key_points.text: Humans learn new concepts by building mental models based on extensive prior knowledge and experience.
The goal of transfer learning is to enable deep learning models to solve new tasks efficiently, even with limited data.
A simple method to give deep learning models access to prior knowledge is to pretrain them on other, related tasks.
Transfer learning involves using a mechanism to transfer knowledge from a pretained network to solve a new, specific task.

key_terms.definition: Transfer learning is a view of learning from little data where the goal is to enable problem solving using minimal data. This approach allows knowledge gained from one task to be applied to a new, related task.
Prior knowledge is the existing information and experience that humans use when learning something new. This knowledge is built from our experience in the world.
Mental model is a model that captures how the world operates, which people build through their experience. Different people can possess different mental models of the world.
Representation is a model that captures how the world operates or what is useful for learning. These representations are what we learn to build upon when acquiring new skills.
Pretrain is the process of training a neural network on other or prior tasks. This allows the network to acquire general knowledge before being applied to a specific new task.

L18.subgoal: Analyze the different types of knowledge transfer and the bottlenecks in implementing them

key_points.text: Knowledge transfer can involve sharing knowledge about model relationships, biases, optimizers, or ethical risks.
A major unsolved problem is building agents that learn intrinsic motivation for efficient exploration and transferring that motivation.
The bottleneck in knowledge transfer is debated as being either fundamentally algorithmic or related to computational efficiency (sample efficiency).
Progress in deep learning has been influenced by both algorithmic ideas and computational efficiency, such as the effective use of GPUs.

key_terms.definition: Intrinsic motivation is a concept where an agent learns internal drives about how to explore its environment. This learned motivation can then be transferred to a new agent to improve its exploration efficiency.
Sample efficiency is a measure of how effectively a learning algorithm uses the data it samples. Poor sample efficiency means that the algorithm requires a large amount of data to learn effectively.

L18.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of fine-tuning and self-supervised pretraining

key_points.text: Transfer learning involves applying knowledge learned from a pretraining task to a related downstream task, often with less data.-
Fine-tuning is the process of initializing a second network with weights and biases from a pre-trained model and then training it on a new task.-
Self-supervised pretraining trains a model to learn data similarity without explicit labels, enabling training on vast amounts of unlabeled data.-
During fine-tuning, the early layers of the model often capture universal features that remain useful across different tasks.-

key_terms.definition: Transferring knowledge is the process of taking knowledge learned from a model trained on one task and applying it to a different, related task. This involves moving the learned structure from the initial model to a new application.
Fine-tuning is a method where a pre-trained network is adapted or refined using a smaller, specific dataset for a new task. This process results in slightly adjusted parameters for the model.

Pretaining is the initial process of training a network's weights and biases on a general, large dataset for a broad task. This results in a set of parameters that can be used as a starting point for subsequent tasks.

Learned representation is the useful, encoded structure captured by a model that is transferred from an initial task. This representation acts as an encoder, capturing useful information about the input data.

Downstream task is the specific, new recognition task that utilizes the useful representation learned from a previous pretraining phase. This is the final application where the transferred knowledge is used to make predictions.

L18.subgoal: Explain how to adapt pre-trained models when input or output dimensions change

key_points.text: When changing input or output dimensions during fine-tuning, new layers (a 'glue') can be added to map data to the required dimensionality.
If only the output dimension changes, the final output layer can be replaced or modified to project the model's representation into the new number of categories.
When adapting a model, the vast majority of the pre-trained structure remains unchanged, and only specific points are modified.
To handle new input dimensions (like RGB-D or hyperspectral data), techniques such as learning an additional encoding or using PCA can be employed.

key_terms.definition: Fine tuning is the process of adapting a pre-trained model to a new, specific task where the input or output structure differs from the original training data. Fine tuning allows the model to leverage existing knowledge while adjusting to new requirements.

Glue is a simple mechanism added into the model structure to transfer data and ensure it is in the correct format for the downstream task. This mechanism is used when the downstream task does not share the same structure as the original pretraining task.

Reprojection is a technique used when only the output dimension of a model changes. Reprojection involves modifying the final output layer of the initial model to project its existing representation into a higher number of dimensions.

Modular building block is a component of a deep learning model that can be taken from one system and inserted into another. This structure allows developers to reuse well-trained components and adapt them to new problems.

L18.subgoal: Describe methods for fine-tuning models and mitigating catastrophic forgetting

key_points.text: Training small models for too long on a new task can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where the model loses its original learned capacity.
To prevent overfitting and forgetting, mechanisms like freezing most of the network or using small learning rates are employed.
Early stopping, based on validation set performance, is a mechanism used to prevent the model from training too much and forgetting the original task.
Because there are no perfect heuristics for custom problems, designing a benchmark is crucial for comparing different model choices and testing performance.

key_terms.definition: Catastrophic forgetting problem occurs when the model's weights change too significantly during training on new data, causing the model to lose the useful knowledge it previously learned from the original data.
Freezing most of the network is a technique where the majority of the model's weights are kept constant, allowing only specific parts, such as the final layers, to be trained for the new task.
Small learning rates are a mechanism that prevents the model from making large adjustments in any direction during training, ensuring that the model moves gradually toward the optimal solution.
Early stopping is a method that utilizes a validation set to decide when to halt training, preventing the model from training excessively and forgetting its original knowledge.

Designing a benchmark involves creating a standardized test environment for a dataset to allow for comparisons across different model choices and observe how those choices affect the model's performance.

L18.subgoal: Describe the mechanisms and motivations behind domain adaptation

key_points.text: Domain adaptation aims to align representation spaces between a source and target domain to improve performance on the target domain [241-244].
One method for alignment is adversarial training, where the model is trained to predict the category while being unable to predict the domain [247-257].
Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is used when the target domain data is available but lacks training labels [262-263].
Domain adaptation models are particularly valuable in scenarios with strong resource constraints, such as remote Arctic sensing [319-322].

key_terms.definition: Domain adaptation is a research area focused on learning a model to perform well on a target domain by ensuring that the representation spaces of the source and target domains are well aligned. This process is often used to address distribution shift problems between different data sources.

Unsupervised domain adaptation is a method where a model is trained to perform well on a set of data without having any training labels available in the target domain. The goal is to leverage labeled source data to improve performance on unlabeled target data.

An adversarial approach involves training a model using both source and target data where the model is simultaneously trained to predict the desired category while being trained to fail at predicting the domain it came from. This mechanism forces the representations across the two domains to align.

Distillation is a mechanism where a student model is trained to predict the same outcome as a teacher model. The student model uses the predictions generated by the teacher model on the target data as weak supervision to learn useful representations.

L18.subgoal: Explain knowledge distillation by matching teacher and student prediction distributions

key_points.text: Knowledge distillation involves training a student model to match the predictions of a fixed, pre-trained teacher model.
Soft targets, derived from the teacher's distribution, are more informative than hard ground truth labels because they convey similarity between categories.
Matching prediction distributions allows the student model to learn context and similarity (e.g., a cat looking like a tiger) rather than just separable categories.
Using soft targets can result in higher test accuracy and less variance in the gradient compared to training with hard targets.

key_terms.definition: Knowledge distillation is a technique where a smaller student model is trained to match the output distribution of a larger, fixed pretrained teacher model. This process allows the student model to learn the knowledge captured in the teacher's predictions.

Soft target is an informative prediction distribution provided by the teacher model, which conveys similarity information between categories. This distribution tells the student model not only the correct class but also how similar the input is to other potential classes.

Cross entropy loss is a function used to train a classifier by minimizing the difference between the model's predicted probability distribution and the true ground truth distribution. This loss function attempts to make the model predict a distribution as close as possible to the actual label.

Teacher model is a large, often pretrained model whose outputs are fixed and used to guide the training of a smaller student model. The teacher model provides the soft targets that the student attempts to replicate.

Student model is the smaller model being trained, whose objective is to learn the knowledge captured in the predictions of the teacher model. Training the student model allows for a more computationally efficient model that retains the performance of the larger teacher.

L18.subgoal: Compare distillation and compression techniques for creating efficient, smaller models

key_points.text: Distillation can be applied across modalities, allowing a student model (e.g., depth) to learn from a teacher model (e.g., RGB) when labeled data is scarce for the student's modality [389-390].
Knowledge distillation can be used to create a smaller, efficient model that matches the output distribution of a large, expensive ensemble of models [396-401].
Representation distillation involves matching internal embeddings (representations) between models using contrastive training, rather than just matching the final output logits [404-405].
Distillation trains a smaller model using SGD to match a large model's characteristics, while compression (pruning/quantization) reduces the computational cost of a large model [438-440].
Specializing a large generalist model to a specific distribution allows for greater quantization and smaller size while maintaining accuracy [451-453].

key_terms.definition: Knowledge distillation is a process where a smaller student model is trained to match the characteristics or outputs of a larger, more complex teacher model. This technique allows the student model to inherit the knowledge of the teacher while being computationally more efficient.

Contrastive learning is a method used to supervise internal embeddings within a model by forcing them to be similar to a target representation. This process is used to ensure that the student model's representation matches the teacher's representation, rather than just matching the final output.

Ensemble is a collection of multiple different models whose combined predictions are often more predictive than any single model. Distillation can be applied to this ensemble by training a single model to match the distribution of the outputs from all the constituent models.

Model compression is a set of mechanisms used to reduce the size of a large machine learning model while maintaining its accuracy. This process is distinct from distillation, which uses training to match characteristics, and includes techniques like pruning or quantization.

Pruning is a method of model compression that involves explicitly removing weights from a model. This technique is highly computationally efficient because it simply deletes parts of the existing model structure.

L18.subgoal: Explain the definition and utility of foundation models in transfer learning

key_points.text: Foundation models are generally useful models effective for a wide variety of downstream tasks.
As foundation models become more general, the requirement for fine-tuning them decreases.
Highly general foundation models are often usable 'off the shelf' without specialized retraining.
The usefulness of a foundation model is related to the percentage of tasks it can perform without specialized training.

key_terms.definition: A foundation model is a generally useful model that is effective across many different downstream tasks. These models are designed to be so broadly useful that they can be applied to a wide variety of problems.

A representation learning model is a type of foundation model where the primary function is learning useful representations. For these models, the question is whether further fine-tuning is necessary to make them useful.
Fine-tuning is the process of adjusting a model after its initial training to make it useful for a specific task. As foundation models become more general, the need for fine-tuning decreases.

A downstream task is a specific application for which a generally useful model can be made effective. These tasks represent the different problems the model is intended to solve after its initial training.

L18.subgoal: Analyze the environmental and societal costs associated with training large foundation models

key_points.text: The size and compute power of AI models have grown exponentially, reaching billions and trillions of parameters (479, 482, 483).
The development of foundation models requires massive financial investment in compute power, which is primarily driven by industry (491, 495).
The carbon emissions of large models are heavily influenced by the sustainability of the data centers' energy sources (502, 503).
Training large models consumes significant amounts of water, raising concerns about global resource access (507, 509, 511).

key_terms.definition: Foundation models are very large models that possess high general utility. These models require massive amounts of compute and resources to train.
Parameters are the numerical values within a model that determine its function. These values can be measured in the billions or trillions for very large models.
Generalizable refers to the ability of a model to perform well on tasks it was not specifically trained for. Very large models are noted to be much more generally useful.
Compute is the amount of computational power required to train or run a model. The increase in compute is tracked as a measure of model growth over time.

L18.subgoal: Explain how prompt engineering adapts large foundation models for new tasks

key_points.text: Foundational models should be viewed as infrastructure, similar to the cost of building an interstate highway system.
Model performance does not significantly improve until much larger model sizes are achieved.
Modern applications often use large language models with little or no data by employing an adapter, such as prompt engineering.
In-context learning involves providing examples to the model to guide its output, which is distinct from the outer loop of supervised pretraining.

key_terms.definition: Prompt engineering is a new paradigm of research where a clever method is used to instruct a large language model to perform tasks for the user. This involves providing specific instructions or examples to guide the model's output, such as asking it to determine the sentiment of a review.
Autoregressively, a model is trained to predict the next character in a sequence based on the characters that came before it. This method is used in models like GPT-3 to generate text sequentially.

In-context learning is an inner loop process where the model is given several examples of the desired task before being asked to continue performing it. This allows the model to learn a task without requiring traditional gradient descent updates.

L18.subgoal: Compare various techniques for adapting and prompting foundation models

key_points.text: Chain-of-thought prompting improves model accuracy by demonstrating reasoning in the answer.
Soft prompting optimizes small continuous task-specific vectors while keeping the language model parameters frozen.
CLIP is a foundation model used for learning semantic similarity between text and images.
Foundation models can be adapted using methods like fine-tuning, learning linear layers, or visual prompting.

key_terms.definition: Soft prompting is a method that optimizes small continuous task-specific vectors while the language or the model parameters remain frozen. Soft prompting essentially attempts to find the optimal input words to use when interacting with the model.

Chain-of-thought prompting is a technique that demonstrates an answer containing reasoning, which encourages the model to answer with logic. This method increases the likelihood that the model will provide a correct answer.

L19.subgoal: Explain how generative models function as a mechanism to access data beyond the original training set

key_points.text: Generative modeling allows a system to sample from the distribution of data it was trained on.
A well-trained generative model can be considered a new mechanism for accessing data, extending beyond the initial training set.
Generative models are essentially a powerful form of data compression.
The Stable Diffusion model demonstrates this concept by compressing humanity's visual information into a few gigabytes.

key_terms.definition: Generative model is a way to capture information about data inputs, allowing the model to sample from the distribution of that data. Generative model can also function as a cool form of data compression.
Meta-learning is the idea of building models that are designed to be good at transfer learning. These models are specifically designed to be good at sharing information or learning new things.
Transfer learning is the process of transferring knowledge, specifically within deep learning models, by focusing on how knowledge about the inputs to the system can be utilized.
Distribution of inputs refers to the expected pattern of the data inputs. Knowing this distribution can be used to direct or accelerate learning or target a specific type of learning.
Latent variable is a concept used in generative models where the model can go from this variable to anything in the dataset. This allows the model to capture all visual information of humanity.

L19.subgoal: Define and explore advanced operations on data objects defined by generative models

key_points.text: Data can be conceptualized as an object involving original data, latent variables, a generative model, and its inverse mapping.
Treating data as an object enables advanced operations, such as interpolation, manipulation, and composition, that are difficult to perform on the raw data itself.
Key operations that can be performed on these data objects include interpolation, manipulation, composition, and optimization.
These mechanisms are applicable to various research domains, including data augmentation, visualization, and counterfactual reasoning.

key_terms.definition: Generative model is the learned mapping (G) that transforms a latent variable into a generated data point. This model is central to the system that generates data.
Latent variable is a set of variables (z) that corresponds to the original training data learned by the generative model. These variables allow for a representation of the original data.
Interpolation is an operator that allows one to generate a new object by interpolating between two different data sets or generators. This process is a standard way of combining data objects.
Manipulation is an operator that allows for changing the data object, such as adding a bias term to the data. This gives a whole new kind of object for accessing and interacting with the data.

Composition is the process of combining two data objects or generators in a way that is distinct from simple interpolation between them. This allows for combining and manipulating data objects in interesting ways.

L19.subgoal: Explain the role of latent variables in controlling generative models

key_points.text: The relationship between movement in latent space and the generated image allows the model to function as a mechanism of control.
Disentangled dimensions in the latent space correspond to specific factors of variation in the real image space, such as pose or orientation.
Explicitly disentangling dimensions of variation in latent space is very difficult and often highly heuristic, especially in high-dimensional spaces.

key_terms.definition: Latent variable is a control point within a latent space that influences the output of a generative model. Latent variables allow the user to control what specific image is synthesized.
Generative model is a function (G) that accepts any point from a latent space and synthesizes a corresponding image. This model is used to create new data based on the input latent variables.

Latent space is the domain containing the latent variables, where movement between points corresponds to changes in the generated image. This space acts as a mechanism of control over the image generation process.

Disentangled factor of variation is a specific dimension within the latent space that corresponds to a clean, independent factor of change in the real generated images. Finding these factors allows for explicit control over specific attributes, such as pose or orientation.

Manifold of natural images is a controllable snippet of the space of natural images that the generative model operates on. Moving along this manifold allows for controlled changes in the generated images.

L19.subgoal: Analyze how latent space exploration can improve robustness while considering its limitations

key_points.text: Building an ensemble over generated variations in the latent space can improve the accuracy and robustness of categorization (,).
Exploring latent space is analogous to performing test time augmentation within the generator itself ().
A core assumption is that points nearby in the image space should reasonably belong to the same category ().
This assumption may fail when attempting fine-grained categorization, such as distinguishing between specific breeds (,,).

key_terms.definition: Latent space is an abstract, compressed representation of the input data where features are organized in a meaningful way. Moving within this space allows for the generation of new, related data points.

Dimensions of variation are measurable and actionable axes within the latent space that correspond to specific changes in the real-world data, such as pose or orientation. These dimensions allow researchers to systematically explore the data manifold.
Manifold is a geometric structure representing the underlying shape of the real image data. The manifold dictates how real images are organized and how variations should naturally occur.

Ensemble is a technique used to improve accuracy and robustness by combining predictions or features derived from multiple generated variations of the input data. This method helps stabilize the categorization process.

Data augmentation is a method used to artificially increase the size and diversity of the training data by creating modified versions of existing inputs. This process helps build robustness into the categorizer.

L19.subgoal: Discover dimensions of variation in latent space using experimental methods

key_points.text: A vector of direction corresponding to a specific counterfactual can be calculated by mapping two images (e.g., same thing at different times) to latent space and finding the vector between them.
Latent space dimensions can correspond to specific image shifts, zooming, brightening, or darkening.
Discovered dimensions often capture specific biases present in the training data, such as assuming dark volcanoes must be erupting.
In word embedding models like Word2Vec, a latent space direction can correspond to changing the tense of a word (e.g., swimming to swam).

key_terms.definition: Latent space is the abstract, compressed representation where data, such as images or words, is mapped. Dimensions of variation are discovered by analyzing how data points are positioned within this space.

Dimensions of variation are specific axes or directions within the latent space that correspond to meaningful changes in the input data. These dimensions allow for controlling specific attributes, such as zooming in, brightening, or darkening an image.

A vector of direction is a calculated vector that represents the path between two mapped points in the latent space. This vector corresponds to a specific type of counterfactual change in the original input data.

Data bias is a specific skew or preference built into the training data that the model learns. This bias causes the model to make specific assumptions, such as assuming an eruption when trying to darken a picture of a volcano.

Word2vec is an embedding model used for words, which maps semantic meanings into a latent space. This model demonstrates how a direction in the latent space can correspond to changing the tense of a word.

L19.subgoal: Explain why interpolating in a latent space preserves the natural image manifold

key_points.text: Disentangled latent space vectors can represent specific factors of variation, such as season or time of day [115-117].
Direct linear interpolation in image space often moves off the natural image manifold, resulting in unrealistic images [129-132].
Interpolating linearly in a well-behaved latent space corresponds to a nonlinear interpolation within the data manifold.
Advanced GANs, like StyleGAN, use intermediate model layers as latent representations, which can be superior to the initial input vector (z) [123-124].

key_terms.definition: Disentangled dimension of variation refers to explicit latent space vectors that separate or factor out different underlying factors of variation within the data. These dimensions allow for the interpretation of specific changes, such as moving from winter to spring.

Generative adversarial network (GAN) is a type of network that allows one to walk in a straight line within a latent space to visualize the resulting data. This visualization technique can sometimes be unreliable or 'cherry picking.'

Natural image manifold is a nonlinear data space, X, that represents the set of real images. Interpolating linearly within this space often results in images that do not match the statistics of real natural images.

Intermediate representation is a layer within a model that can itself function as a latent space. These representations are sometimes found to be better latent representations than the initial input vector (z representation).

L19.subgoal: Explain why intermediate latent spaces improve data interpolation and disentanglement

key_points.text: Linear interpolation across seams in the standard latent space (z space) can result in unnatural or jarring shifts in the generated data.
Using an intermediate representation, such as the 'w space,' can help avoid distorted areas and seams, leading to more realistic interpolation.
Intermediate spaces, demonstrated by StyleSpace, can successfully isolate and disentangle dimensions of variation, such as body color or hood styles.

key_terms.definition: Natural image manifold is the space where real-world images reside, representing the distribution of natural data. It defines the boundaries of what constitutes a realistic image.
Latent distribution is the probability distribution that maps to the data distribution within a generative model. It serves as the compressed representation of the input data.

Linear interpolation is a method of smoothly transitioning between two points in a space by moving along a straight line. When performed across certain boundaries, it can result in unnatural or jarring shifts in the generated data.

Intermediate representation is a space located between the original data and the latent space that is less distorted. This space is beneficial because it is less likely to contain problematic seams or danger zones.

Disentangled dimensions of variation are independent factors of change within the data, such as hood styles or body colors. These dimensions can be isolated and controlled by moving to a more intermediate space.

L19.subgoal: Explain how generative models can be used to efficiently label synthetic data

key_points.text: Points that are close together in the generative model's manifold should be semantically related, allowing for label transfer.
The DatasetGAN paper used StyleGAN to efficiently generate large datasets of images and corresponding semantic segmentation labels.
The efficiency of the GAN approach was demonstrated by showing that one labeled GAN image was equivalent to about 100 labeled regular images.
Modern semantic segmentation often utilizes foundation models like SAM, which rely on self-supervision techniques.

key_terms.definition: Semantic segmentation is a task where the goal is to label parts of an image, assigning specific labels to individual pixels. This process is often expensive and slow, especially when dealing with fine-grained object boundaries.

Latent space is a well-behaved, aligned representation space learned by a generative model. This space organizes data such that dimensions of variation and similarity are maintained, making features more semantically meaningful than raw pixels.
Generative model is a type of model trained on existing data to create new, synthetic data. The argument is that things close together in the manifold of this model should be semantically related.

StyleGAN is a generative model used in this context to efficiently label data. It is employed to generate a representation of specific pixel vectors that can then be used to train a predictive model for part labels.

Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a modern segmentation model that relies on building a very large dataset. This model uses self-supervision and specific augmentation techniques to learn a generalizable and robust segmentation capability.

L19.subgoal: Apply latent space manipulation to probe model predictions and underlying data biases

key_points.text: Generative models can be used to increase the interpretability of model dimensions and explain predictions.
Interpretability can be achieved by perturbing the latent space to understand how changes affect the model's prediction.
StylEx identifies top latent space directions that most influence which class the model predicts.
Probing the model using latent space manipulation can reveal underlying biases present in the training data.

key_terms.definition: A generative model is a type of model whose data plus plus approach can teach how to explain things or increase the interpretability of certain dimensions. It is used to create a data plus plus space for analysis.
Data plus plus space is a space derived from generative models where one can explore counterfactuals. This space allows researchers to understand why an image was classified in a certain way.

Latent space is the internal, compressed representation of data where researchers can explicitly perturb variables. This allows them to understand how changes in the representation affect a model's prediction.

StyleSpace explanation approach is a method that attempts to find the top K latent space directions of variation. These directions are chosen because they will most significantly affect which class a model predicts.

Underlying bias in training data refers to dimensions of bias captured by the model. These dimensions reflect patterns present in the training data itself, such as the correlation between ear shape and species.

L19.subgoal: Apply explainability to medical data and evaluate modern counterfactual methods

key_points.text: Explainability mechanisms can reveal dimensions of bias learned by a model, such as linking specific features to perceived age or characteristics.
Explainability techniques can be applied to scientific or medical data, such as retinal fundus images, to understand disease categorization.
Using explainability in medical contexts helps build trust because expert doctors can validate the model's predictive features.
Manually discovering latent space variations is difficult, but modern diffusion models use text conditioning to efficiently test counterfactual hypotheses.

key_terms.definition: Dimensions of variation are specific features or attributes within the data that the model learns correspond to certain types of predictions. These dimensions can be used to probe how a model is making its predictions.

Dimensions of bias are specific variations that capture biases, which may be related to the fairness or equity of a deployed model. These dimensions can be analyzed to understand how they affect a model's predictions.

An explainability mechanism is a method used to understand how a model functions, allowing experts to verify if the model is using appropriate features. This process can build trust in a model by confirming its reasoning.

Latent space variation refers to the hidden, underlying variations within the data that must be discovered and manually analyzed. Finding these variations requires significant effort to understand the model's behavior.

Counterfactual reasoning is a method of understanding or testing hypotheses by generating possible alternative scenarios. This allows researchers to efficiently test how a model performs given different hypothetical data changes.

L19.subgoal: Analyze how generative models and architectural design contribute knowledge beyond raw data

key_points.text: Generated data can potentially be useful for representation learning, similar to real data (262, 263).
A core debate exists regarding whether a generator can extract more information than the underlying data itself (283, 284).
Architectural design, such as convolutional neural networks, fundamentally injects knowledge beyond the raw intermediate data (286, 287).
Data augmentation techniques can be viewed as a mechanism that builds explicit assumptions about data structure, similar to a learned generative model (290, 294).
A refined approach for contrastive learning involves transforming images by moving slightly in latent space along the image manifold (306).

key_terms.definition: A generative model is a type of model trained on a dataset to capture the underlying information, potentially generating new data that is useful for representation learning. This model aims to capture either the same information as the dataset or arguably slightly more.

Representation learning is the process of learning useful representations from data, which can potentially be improved by using generated data. This process aims to create a representation space that effectively distinguishes between different categories.

Contrastive learning is a training method that aims to learn a representation space where images from the same category are close together, while images from different categories are far apart. This is achieved by training a contrastive style loss.

Data augmentation is an engineering mechanism that manipulates data during training, such as random flipping or cut and paste, to increase the robustness of machine learning models. This mechanism builds explicit assumptions about how objects relate to backgrounds.

The image manifold is the space that represents the manifold of real images, which can be used to guide transformations in latent space. Moving within this manifold allows for transformations that maintain fidelity to the real image data.

L19.subgoal: Analyze the theoretical robustness and diversity-fidelity trade-offs in contrastive learning

key_points.text: The model can still learn useful representations even when false positive or negative characterizations exist in the training data.
Contrastive learning can construct positive pairs by taking latent views—moving within a ball around the real image—instead of using standard augmentations like cropping or warping.
A critical challenge in training signals is balancing the trade-off between diversity and fidelity.
It is generally more useful for learning if two things that are significantly different are identified as the same, compared to two things that are almost identical.

key_terms.definition: Latent space is a compressed, high-dimensional representation of the input data where the model learns features. Movement within this space corresponds to changes in the data representation.

Contrastive learning is a mechanism for training models where the objective is to ensure that representations of similar data points are close together while representations of dissimilar data points are pushed far apart.
Positive pairs are pairs of data views that are considered similar because they originate from the same underlying input image, used to train contrastive learning algorithms.
Regularization is a mechanism that helps prevent models from overfitting by introducing noise or constraints during the training process.
Diversity versus fidelity is a trade-off in training signal usefulness, balancing whether the training samples are highly different from each other (diversity) or nearly identical (fidelity).

L19.subgoal: Analyze the challenges of defining class boundaries and how generative methods can improve representation learning

key_points.text: Defining class boundaries requires representative data from all dimensions of real variation, which is often missing in few-shot learning scenarios.
The philosophical concept of categorization may be limited, as fixed lists of attributes can always be broken by counterexamples.
Incorporating movement within the latent space (generative views) can significantly boost contrastive learning performance compared to using only real data.
Deep learning models tend to learn strong shape priors, making it difficult to change shape compared to changing texture.

key_terms.definition: Latent space is the space where image feature vectors are moved and manipulated during generation. Moving around this space allows for variations in an image while attempting to maintain its core characteristics.

Class boundary is the limit in the latent space where moving further causes the generated image to cross into a different category. Understanding this boundary is crucial for defining the reasonable limits of a specific class.

Few shot learning is difficult because it often means there is no well-understood representation space of the boundaries of a real class. This lack of knowledge about boundaries makes it challenging to generalize effectively.

Contrastive learning is a method of training models that uses real data based on a set of heuristic rules that are designed not to break the class boundary. This contrasts with using generative data based on experimental parameter setups.

L19.subgoal: Analyze the challenges, trade-offs, and risks associated with using generation-augmented data

key_points.text: Generative models can be used to augment data, allowing for operations like interpolation, manipulation, and efficient labeling.
Generative models can be used to efficiently probe for biases in large datasets by interacting with the system using text.
Optimizing generative data for test metrics may not translate to better performance in real-world, open-ended scenarios.
Training models on an excessive ratio of generated data compared to real data can lead to model collapse, causing the loss of real data distribution.

key_terms.definition: Implicit generative model is a type of model that allows sampling from a complex data distribution without explicitly defining the probability density function. This model can be used as a mechanism to generate data with extra functionality.

Generation-augmented data is data that has been enhanced or supplemented using a generative model. This type of data allows for applying standard data operations, such as interpolation or manipulation, to potentially label data efficiently.

Model collapse is a vicious cycle that occurs when a model is trained on more generated data than real data. This process can cause the model to lose parts of its original distribution that were present in the real data.

Manifold collapse is a related phenomenon where the model loses parts of its distribution due to the nature of the generated data. This occurs when the training data heavily favors the distribution of the generated output.

Bias refers to systematic prejudices or correlations present within the training data. Detecting bias involves figuring out if the training data correlates certain features, such as darkness, with specific outcomes, even if those correlations are not visually obvious.

L19.subgoal: Compare MAML's inner/outer loop approach with sequence modeling for meta-learning

key_points.text: MAML attempts to learn an initialization that is easily adaptable using only a few steps of stochastic gradient descent.
The MAML algorithm involves a double loop optimization, requiring backpropagation through the inner loop of SGD.
Meta-learning models can be computationally expensive, often making simple pretraining a more practical choice.
Sequence modeling, such as in autoregressive models, can function as a mechanism of meta-learning through in-context learning.

key_terms.definition: Meta-learning is the process of learning a model that is effective at transfer learning, allowing the model to adapt quickly to new tasks.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) is a seminal work that attempts to learn an initial set of parameters such that the model can be easily adapted using only a few steps of stochastic gradient descent.
In-context learning is a mechanism of meta-learning where the model learns to generate answers by being provided a sequence of input and ground truth examples.
Sequence modeling is a definition of learning where the model processes a sequence of input and ground truth data to output a function capable of generating new ground truth for novel inputs.

L20.subgoal: Define scaling laws and understand their predictive power in deep learning

key_points.text: Scaling laws are predictions that describe how a model will behave when resources like compute or model size are scaled.
Identifying these laws is useful for planning resources and predicting the future competence of deep learning models.
The research presented is cutting-edge and empirical, meaning the results are ongoing and may not stand the test of time.
The amount of compute used to train deep learning models is increasing exponentially over time, similar to Moore's law.

key_terms.definition: Scaling laws are predictions that describe how a model will behave when its resources are changed, such as doubling the compute or doubling the model size. These laws are useful for planning resources and making extrapolations into the future.

L20.subgoal: Understand the importance of scaling laws, referencing 'The Bitter Lesson.'

key_points.text: Richard Sutton's 'The Bitter Lesson' suggests that simple algorithms that scale well are the ones that systematically succeed in AI.
Scaling laws are related to asymptotic analysis, which is a foundational concept in computer science (e.g., Big O notation).
Asymptotic analysis determines how an algorithm's time complexity scales as a function of the input complexity.
Predicting future model behavior requires understanding how things scale, as current trends show continuous scaling.

key_terms.definition: Scaling law is a principle that describes how a model's or algorithm's behavior changes as a function of increasing resources or input complexity. Scaling laws are used to predict how models will perform in the future.

Asymptotic analysis is a standard computer science idea that examines how a property of a model scales when resources, complexity, or an input parameter increases. This analysis is necessary for making predictions about how things will scale.
Time complexity is a measure of how the time required by an algorithm to run scales as a function of the input complexity. This concept is used to understand how an algorithm's behavior scales.

L20.subgoal: Explain the strategy for efficiently designing and training large models using scaling laws

key_points.text: The fundamental question of scaling laws is how to optimally allocate a budget of compute or hardware to train a model.
Compute is measured in FLOPs (floating point operations), which can be allocated sequentially or in parallel.
Companies design and test models at small scales, extrapolate the performance curve, and then train only once at the massive scale.
For scaling laws, performance is typically predicted at a given compute level using the optimal amount of data for that compute level.

key_terms.definition: Scaling law is a fundamental question in the study of deep learning that addresses how to optimally allocate a budget of compute or hardware to determine the best model and data usage.
Compute is the total computational resource budget, which is measured in floating point operations (flops) on the hardware.
Flops (Floating Point Operations) is the unit used to measure compute, representing the number of floating point operations performed on the hardware.
Performance is a measure of the model's quality, which is quantified in bits per word and relates to the cross-entropy of the next-word prediction.
Cross-entropy of the next-word prediction is a metric related to the model's accuracy, where a lower value indicates that the model is making more accurate predictions.

L20.subgoal: Differentiate between scaling laws applied to training loss versus downstream performance

key_points.text: Scaling laws can predict trends in downstream performance, not just the training loss.
Scaling laws are predictive models that relate a parameter of interest (like test loss) to critical resources (data, compute, parameters).
A primary application of scaling laws is determining the optimal number of parameters (N) and data points (D) for a fixed compute budget (C).
The required compute (C) to train a model is roughly proportional to the product of the number of parameters (N) and the number of data points (D).

key_terms.definition: Scaling laws are trends that attempt to predict a specific parameter of interest, such as test loss, as a function of critical resources like data, compute, or model size. These laws help inform how to select resources to achieve the lowest possible test loss.

Downstream performance refers to the predictive capability of a model on specific tasks or benchmarks, such as passing math tests or coding problems, rather than just the training loss. Scaling laws can be applied to predict trends in this type of performance.

Parameters (N) represent the number of adjustable variables within a model, which is one of the critical resources used to predict performance. The number of parameters is generally looked at as a function of resources.

Data points (D) refers to the number of individual examples used in the training dataset, which is a critical resource for scaling. This term specifically refers to the quantity of data, not dimensionality or depth.

Compute budget (C) is the total computational effort, measured in flops, required to train a model of a specific size on a given dataset. This budget is used to determine the optimal number of parameters and data points.

L20.subgoal: Identify the core problem of optimizing model size and data size under a fixed compute budget

key_points.text: Given a fixed compute budget, the goal is to maximize performance (minimize loss) by determining the optimal balance between model size and data size.
The idea of scaling laws for neural networks was popularized by a paper from Jared Kaplan and Sam McCandlish at OpenAI.
The computational cost of training models is measured in FLOPs, not in dollars.
The foundational paper studied various factors, including model size, dataset size (D), and the shape of the network.
The paper on scaling laws is assigned as reading because it provides a beautiful piece of science and great insight into the research process.

key_terms.definition: Flops is the unit of measurement used to quantify the total computational effort or compute budget required for training a model. It is the metric that the scaling laws paper focused on for analyzing resource allocation.
Next-character prediction is the specific task used in the study, which involves predicting the character that follows the current character in a sequence.
Autoregressive transformer model is a type of language model that utilizes a transformer architecture and predicts data sequentially, such as character by character.
Data set size (D) refers to the total quantity of tokens or data points that the model is trained on.

L20.subgoal: Define and explain the power law scaling relationship between loss and resources

key_points.text: The main finding is that test loss relates to resources (parameters, data points, or compute) via a power law relationship.
This power law relationship is expressed as Loss being proportional to one over the resource value raised to the alpha exponent.
The exponent alpha is a constant that depends on the specific properties of the data, task, and architecture.
If resources are doubled, the loss decreases by $2^{-\alpha}$.

key_terms.definition: Power law relationship is a type of relationship where the test loss and the resources used are connected by a specific mathematical function. This relationship is expressed as one over the resource value raised to the alpha exponent.

Alpha is a constant parameter within the power law that determines the shape of the relationship. This constant depends on the specific properties of the data, the task, or the architecture being used.

Compute is the total computational effort required for training, which is approximated by multiplying the number of parameters by the number of data points. This approximation is used to estimate the resources needed for the training process.

Test loss is the metric used to evaluate the model's performance, and it is shown to follow a power law relationship with the resources used during training. This loss value is the dependent variable in the scaling law.

L20.subgoal: Explain the empirical power law relationship between data set size and test loss

key_points.text: Empirically, there exists a power law relationship between data set size and test loss.
The test loss is modeled as a function of data set size following the form 1 over data set size to the alpha, where alpha is empirically about 0.1.
A power law relationship is represented as a straight line on a log-log plot, where the slope equals the exponent.
The observed scaling laws are specific to the chosen model family and may not extrapolate to other models.

key_terms.definition: Power law relationship is an empirical finding where a relationship exists between data set size and test loss, following a specific mathematical form.
Log-log plot is a type of graph where both the x-axis and y-axis are plotted using logarithms, allowing a power law to appear as a straight line whose slope equals the power law's exponent.
Test loss is the metric plotted on the y-axis, which measures the performance of the model on unseen data.
Data set size is the independent variable plotted on the x-axis, representing the total number of tokens the model is trained on.
Cross-entropy is a specific type of loss function, often used in next-word prediction tasks, which is one of the functions observed to follow power laws.

L20.subgoal: Analyze the empirical and theoretical basis of scaling laws

key_points.text: The observed power law relationship in deep learning is primarily empirical, not derived from first principles.
The theoretical basis for scaling laws emerges from high-dimensional statistics.
Power laws are general and show up for all kinds of data distributions.
The conclusion that a power law exists often results from plotting empirical data points and finding a line on a log-log plot.

key_terms.definition: Power law relationship is a mathematical relationship observed in data where the points form a straight line when plotted on a log-log plot, indicating a specific scaling behavior.
High-dimensional statistics is a field of study where the dependence on dimensionality influences the function fitting process, which can result in a specific scaling exponent.
Empirical describes observations that are derived from actual measurements of data, rather than being derived from theoretical first principles.

L20.subgoal: Describe the Pareto front that defines optimal scaling across compute, data, and parameters

key_points.text: Scaling compute or data set size results in a power law relationship with test loss.
The power laws for scaling compute and data have different slopes and constant offsets.
The Pareto front represents the frontier of optimal performance achieved by scaling compute, data, and parameters simultaneously.
To observe the power law, one must optimally tune the data set size and parameters for every level of compute.

key_terms.definition: Power law is a mathematical relationship where the test loss behaves as a power law when scaled with respect to compute or data set size. This relationship is characterized by a specific constant offset and a specific slope.

Pareto front is the frontier that represents the optimal trade-offs among all different curves for various specific models and training configurations. This frontier is achieved when optimally using infinitely large data sets or selecting the perfect model size.

L20.subgoal: Explain how model size and data size interact to achieve optimal performance

key_points.text: Increasing compute on a fixed dataset and model eventually causes the loss to plateau.
To observe power law performance improvements, the model size and dataset size must scale together.
The test loss (L) can be modeled as a function of both the number of parameters (N) and the dataset size (D).
The scaling laws are based on empirical measurements and are not derived from theory in the paper.

key_terms.definition: Power law relationship is a mathematical relationship where one factor's performance scales proportionally to a power of another factor, assuming all other variables are set optimally. This relationship is observed between factors like model size, data set size, and performance.
Loss is the metric used to measure the performance of the model, which is plotted against training factors to observe scaling behavior. The goal of training is to achieve a lower loss.
Model capacity is the inherent ability of a model to find a specific fit, which is limited by its structure. For example, a linear model only has enough capacity to find a linear fit.

L20.subgoal: Apply the derived scaling laws to optimize model training resources

key_points.text: The three fundamental resources governing training are model size, data set size, and compute (number of steps).
The relationship between test loss and the fundamental resources can be modeled as the sum of two power laws.
To minimize loss given a fixed compute resource (C), the number of parameters should be proportional to C to the 0.7.
To minimize loss given a fixed compute resource (C), the number of data points should be proportional to C to the 0.27.
The implication of these laws is that training relatively large models on relatively small data is optimal for minimizing test loss.

key_terms.definition: Compute is one of the three fundamental resources used in training models, calculated by multiplying the number of steps taken by the batch size.
Test loss is the metric that the researchers found a simpler functional form for explaining the relationship between it and the model's parameters and data size.
Power law is a functional form that describes the relationship between the test loss and the model's parameters or the number of steps of gradient descent.
Model size is one of the three fundamental resources, referring to the number of parameters in the model.
Frontier is the boundary of performance that is reached when the number of parameters is increased sufficiently.

L20.subgoal: Evaluate the predictive power of scaling laws across different domains like computer vision

key_points.text: Power laws are observed in various fields, including computer vision and reinforcement learning, not just autoregressive transformers.
The relationship between loss, dataset size, and model size can be modeled as the sum of two power laws.
These power laws are predictive and extrapolate across orders of magnitude, meaning they are not merely descriptive observations.

key_terms.definition: Power law is a relationship where performance scales according to a specific mathematical function of resources. Power law describes how performance relates to resources, such as data set size or model size.
Loss is a metric used to quantify the error of a model's predictions. Loss is plotted on the vertical axis when analyzing how model performance changes with resource scaling.

Extrapolate is the ability of a model to make valid predictions outside the range of data it was trained on. Extrapolation determines if a model's fitted relationship holds true across orders of magnitude.

Cross-validation is an experimental technique used to assess how well a model generalizes to unseen data. Cross-validation confirms that the observed power law relationship is not merely a coincidence of the training data.

L21.subgoal: Explain the relationship between LLMs and the evolution of deep learning

key_points.text: LLMs are built on deep nets, but they are also considered a potential next paradigm beyond traditional deep learning characteristics.
LLMs possess new fundamental math and characteristics that extend beyond continuous weight updates and standard MLPs and ConvNets.
The lecture will focus on the capabilities of language generation systems rather than the specific details of the underlying architecture.
Students interested in LLMs are encouraged to take related courses, such as 6.8610.

key_terms.definition: Large language model (LLM) is a system built upon deep nets that is considered a potential next paradigm following deep learning. LLMs are viewed as a major subject deserving of dedicated study.
Next token prediction is the process of generating language by predicting the subsequent token in a sequence. This capability is central to building language generation systems.

Paradigm is a fundamental shift in thinking or operation that goes beyond existing methods, such as deep learning. This new paradigm possesses characteristics and fundamental math that differ from traditional deep learning approaches.
Deep net is the foundational architecture upon which large language models are built. Large language models are essentially made out of these deep nets.

L21.subgoal: Define language models and describe early count-based approaches

key_points.text: A language model predicts the next word in a distribution given a sequence of input words or tokens.,
By predicting the next word, a model can generate language by creating a distribution over strings.
Historically, language models were estimated by counting word occurrences within large text corpora.
Using longer contexts when counting leads to a better ability to generate text that resembles natural language.,

key_terms.definition: Count-based language model is an earlier generation of tool that estimates probabilities by getting big text corpora and counting word occurrences. These models were used to determine the plausibility of a particular decoding or sequence.
Text corpora is a large collection of text used to estimate probabilities in language models by counting the number of times specific word sequences occur.

L21.subgoal: Explain the factors driving the improvement in language model prediction accuracy

key_points.text: Neural network models initially provided a modest improvement in perplexity over classical count-based models for next word prediction.-
The current standard for next word prediction in the modern era is the transformer architecture.
The significant improvement in language model prediction ability is attributed to better prediction machinery and larger data sets.
Between 2000 and 2020, advancements allowed for training much larger models with more parameters on larger datasets.-

key_terms.definition: Perplexity is a measure used to evaluate the quality of a language model's predictions. Perplexity quantifies how well a language model performs when predicting the next word in a sequence.

L21.subgoal: Compare historical and modern language models, focusing on the role of architecture

key_points.text: Early large language models, despite having massive parameters and data, were generally less effective than modern neural models.
The inductive bias provided by neural sequence models is a critical factor in their superior performance compared to previous language models.
Historically, language models were typically used as auxiliary tools to rerank outputs within larger pipeline systems, rather than performing tasks independently.
Around 2014, the field shifted to using language models to perform tasks autonomously, such as framing machine translation as a next-word prediction problem.

key_terms.definition: Large language model is a type of model that can be trained on massive amounts of data and parameters, capable of performing complex tasks like sequence generation. These models demonstrate that superior performance is not solely dependent on the sheer quantity of data or parameters.

N-gram counts are the parameters used in older language models, representing the frequency counts of sequences of words. These counts were utilized in early language models, such as the one referenced in the literature.

Inductive bias is a special characteristic inherent in neural sequence models that allows them to perform better than previous generations of language models. This bias is a key factor contributing to the success of modern neural models.

Sequence generation is the process where a language model is used to perform a task by generating a sequence of outputs, rather than merely ranking candidates. This shift allowed language models to be used directly for tasks like machine translation.

Next word prediction problem is a method where a language model is framed to guess the subsequent word in a sequence. This framing allows the model to be applied to tasks like translating a sentence from one language to another.

L21.subgoal: Explain the evolution of NLP training from single-task models to transfer learning

key_points.text: Since 2017, the most significant changes in language modeling have been in the training procedures, rather than the models themselves.
Transfer learning allows models to be pre-trained on a large dataset for a general task (like next word prediction) and then fine-tuned for a specific downstream task using much less data.
The current era of pretraining and prompting seeks to utilize general-purpose systems without needing to modify the model's parameters for every new task.
Masked Language Modeling (MLM) is a pretraining task where the model predicts hidden words in a text based on the surrounding context.
MLM is effective because it allows models to learn the structure and meaning of language without requiring labeled task-specific data.

key_terms.definition: Next word prediction is a general purpose task where a model is trained to predict the subsequent word in a sequence of text. This task serves as a foundational system that can be leveraged for various downstream applications.

Masked language modeling is a pretraining objective where the model receives text input and is tasked with predicting words that have been intentionally hidden within that text. This objective allows the model to be trained using only readily available text without needing any labeled task-specifics

Pretrain and transfer mode is an operational style where a model is first trained extensively on massive amounts of text data. Subsequently, the model is adapted to a specific downstream task using only a small amount of data.

Fine-tuning is the process of adapting a pre-trained model to perform a specific task of interest. This adaptation is typically achieved by using a hidden representation from one of the model's layers for the new task.

Pretraining and prompting is the current era of language model development where a highly general purpose next word prediction system is utilized. This allows for performing tasks without needing to modify the model's parameters or requiring downstream task data.

L21.subgoal: Explain how simple masked language modeling leads to complex NLP capabilities

key_points.text: Large-scale training on masked language modeling allows models to be fine-tuned successfully on various complex NLP tasks like sentiment analysis and entailment.
Doing a good job of predicting words in context requires the model to possess a huge amount of linguistic knowledge, such as grammatical agreement and tense.
To perform well, models must also acquire and memorize contingent world knowledge and facts from the training text.
Training on vast amounts of text allows models to embody this linguistic and world knowledge within their internal parameters.

key_terms.definition: Masked language modeling objective is a specific pretraining task where the model is trained to predict words that have been intentionally hidden or masked within a sentence. This objective allows the model to learn deep contextual relationships between words.

Large scale transfer effects describe the ability of a model to apply general knowledge learned during massive pretraining to perform well on smaller, specific downstream tasks. This capability is what makes pretraining effective for various NLP applications.

Word embeddings are representations of words learned at the input layer of a system. Evidence showed that these embeddings could provide good transfer effects, allowing models to generalize knowledge.

Fine-tuning is the process of taking a large, pre-trained model and adapting it to perform well on a very small, specific task. This allows the model to leverage its general knowledge while specializing in a particular application.

Pretraining is the initial phase of training a model on a massive amount of general text data. This process enables the model to embody a vast amount of linguistic and world knowledge in its internal parameters.

L21.subgoal: Compare the limitations of Masked Language Modeling with the requirements for text generation

key_points.text: Masked language modeling (MLM) models are not designed to generate the next word in a sequence because they are trained to predict missing words in the middle of a sentence.
Bidirectional transformer models provide good representations but cannot be directly used for text generation.
The effective paradigm for text generation involved combining general pretraining (like MLM) with models that predict the next word in a sequence.
This combined pretraining and generation paradigm was the standard approach for a long time, used for tasks like translation and summarization.

key_terms.definition: Masked language modeling paradigm is a training setup where the model is trained to predict missing words, which often appear in the middle of a sentence. This paradigm does not result in a model that can actually generate the next word sequentially at the end of a sentence.
Bidirectional transformer models are models that produce good representations of text. However, these models were not inherently capable of performing text generation.

Text generation is the process of creating textual output, such as in machine translation or summarization. This capability often requires a second stage that is trained specifically to generate the text.
Pretraining paradigm refers to the initial training phase of a model using a large amount of data. This phase aims to create a highly effective model before it is specialized for a particular task.

Conditional text generation is a type of text generation where the model is designed to output text based on specific input conditions. Models that perform this task are capable of predicting the next word in a sequence.

L21.subgoal: Describe the shift from fine-tuning to using context to control language models

key_points.text: Large language models can perform surprising tasks, such as arithmetic or multilingual question answering, without needing targeted fine-tuning once they reach a certain scale.
The primary way to exert control over a language model today is by changing the input or context provided to it, rather than by fine-tuning.
In-context learning is a powerful tool used to change the context and get language models to exhibit desired target behaviors.

key_terms.definition: In-context learning is a powerful tool used to change the context of a language model in order to get the model to exhibit desired target behaviors. This mechanism allows control over a text generation system by changing the input provided to it.

Downstream fine-tuning is a method where a pre-trained model is used as a starting point for subsequent tasks. This process typically involves adjusting the model to perform specific tasks after initial training.

L21.subgoal: Explain why standard next-token prediction fails for classification and how in-context learning solves it

key_points.text: Standard next-token prediction is often unsuitable for specific labeling tasks (like sentiment classification) because the desired label is statistically unlikely to follow the input text.
In-context learning, or few-shot prompting, is a method used to adapt a language model to a specific labeling task by specifying expected outputs.
